title: Introducing Aubrey Alexander-Your 2013 Female Counselor
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello 2013 ILE’ers!
My name is Aubrey Alexander and I live in Emporia, Kansas.  I’m currently studying to be a High School Biology Teacher, so this summer will give me some great practice working with teenagers.
My great grandmother’s name was Kathleen McNamara and it was her dream to see her love of Ireland carried on through her generations.  She made sure all of her grandchildren, my father included, had the opportunity to visit the land she loved and form a deeper relationship with our treasured heritage.  My father experienced Ireland through the ILE Program and just as his grandmother intended; fell in love with the land and its people.  In 2007, my father in turn, sent me to Ireland with the same program and his grandmother’s dream continued.  The same with my sister in 2010-it’s a family tradition.  It was love at first sight for all of us!
My adventure with the Irish Life Experience was quite possibly the best summer of my life!  I made great friends that I sill keep in touch with, but what changed me the most was Ireland itself.  It is a magical place, and its rich history and beauty touched my heart and soul.  Through this special program, I formed a relationship with the Emerald Isle and it is truly where my heart will always belong.  
A few random facts about me…  In my spare time, I love to run.  It is probably my favorite past time.  I feel free when I run and it helps me clear my head.  I especially love it when the weather outside is nice and I can run some place beautiful and enjoy the outdoors.  I’m also a coffee lover-Caramel Macchiato anyone?  And if you bring me a coffee, I will pretty much fall in love with you and be your best friend for life!  If I could get paid to read books, I think that would be the best job in the world.  Chelsea Handler and Jenna Marble are my two favorite blondes.  I think they are hilarious.  My boyfriend says I have a soft spot for kittens and ice cream.  He’s kind of right.  I love him, summertime, and country music.  
I can’t wait to meet all of you in a few short weeks.  Ireland is going to be so much fun!  This may be my new best summer ever!

title: YOLO-Or #YOIIO!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
So…, being that I’m a little behind on pop culture, I just discovered what YOLO meant last summer during the Irish Life Experience.  For those of you who don’t know, YOLO is the acronym for the phrase, “You Only Live Once,” which is often used as a hashtag on Twitter to bring attention to exciting events.  
The acronym first started popping up around 2004, when Adam Mesh, from the NBC reality show, the Average Joe, launched a clothing line called YOLO.  Since then, it’s been used in a few places sporadically.  On Urban Dictionary, for a promotional website for San Francisco’s nightlife, and by the American Indie rock band-The Strokes.  Then in the Fall of 2011, Canadian recording artist Drake, used the acronym in his new hip hop single, “The Motto.”  On December 16th, 2011, The Huffington Post published a photo of American actor, Zac Efron (My future husband.) with YOLO tattooed on his right hand and in March of 2012 a Facebook page for YOLO already had 3,725 likes.  Impressive to say the least!
So…, when the Irish Life Experience landed in Ireland last summer, there were many YOLO’s said as every day was exciting.  However, a few amazing students (The Dream Team) coined a new motto.  YOIIO-You’re Only In Ireland Once.  How perfect!  Now, we know that many of our alumni will return to Ireland again, and again, and again.  However, if you study abroad in Ireland with the Irish Life Experience, #YOIIO will forever be your new motto.

title: Celtic Warriors
author: tharrison
content_raw:
1, 2, 3, Jab, 1, 2, 3, Hook, 1, 2, 3, Punch.  
While the US has the Dream Team and the Fab Five, Ireland has the Celtic Warriors-boxers Katie Taylor, John Joe Nevin, Paddy Barnes, and Michael Conlan?
On August 9th, slugger Katie Taylor won Ireland’s first Olympic gold medal since 1996, when Michelle Smith won three gold and one bronze medal in Atlanta for swimming.  A few days later, John Joe Nevin-a sliver, Paddy Barnes and Michael Conlan-both a bronze.  Success all around in the ring!
Team Ireland returned home from London, after its most successful Olympics since 1956.  On Monday, 66 Irish athletes were welcomed by their relatives at Dublin Airport, before returning to their hometowns.  Katie Taylor was welcomed by 20 thousand people gathered along the seafront of her home, in Bray, Co. Wexford.  There were 6,000 people waiting for John Joe Nevin in Cusak Park in Mullingar, Co. Westmeath, while the bronze medal winners of Barnes and Conlan, were greeted to a reception at the Titanic Center in Belfast.
Michael Ring, Minister of State for Tourism and Sport, thanked the team on behalf of the Government and the Irish people.  “You lifted the souls, minds, and hearts of the people in Ireland during this difficult economic climate,” Ring said.  
The Guinness was flowing and there was much to be celebrated on the Emerald Isle this week.  Meanwhile, the Celtic Warriors are already looking ahead to Rio 2016.

author: tharrison
content_raw:
And so begins our first full day of holiday time in Galway.
With the kids settled in to their wonderful apartments in Gort na Corribe in Galway city and having had a great night’s sleep, we all stepped on the bus for a tour to County Clare, home of Brian Farrell, owner of Burren Coaches who was with us for the Killarney leg of the trip, and home of Liam’s family.
We set off at 10am and en route dropped Liam to meet his uncle who was taking him to visit his family in Ennis, Co Clare for the day. Angie and Taryn met Uncle John, who is a lovely man and was very excited to have Liam visit for the day.
With Angie as our tour guide we were treated to the joys of her vast knowledge of the area and her tales and information which is not listed in any guide book but rather handed down from local people. We passed through Clarenbridge which is famous for its 50 year old Oyster Festival. The next town was called Kinvarra and Angie told the story of Dunguaire Castle whose ruins stand at the entrance to the town and dates back to 1520. Kinvarra is also famous for the Galway Hookers which are traditional Irish boats. The kids had a giggle when Angie explained exactly what they were!
We also passed through Ballyvaughan, a lively picturesque town well known for traditional Irish music and Irish cuisine.
Our first stop was in the Burren for a walking tour and mountain hike which gave the most beautiful views of the countryside. The Burren is famous for being the origin of over 70% of Ireland’s flora and more famous for its beautiful, unusual landscape which is mainly limestone and has a purple hue when the sun shines – which hasn’t been too often on this trip but we touched lucky today for a few hours! It was great to get some fresh air and exercise and for the staff to work off all that extra Cadbury’s chocolate and Twister lollies they have been eating.
Off we trotted to the bus again after a great walk that Angie totally ruined by having a massive slice of carrot cake with fresh cream  – it was home baked, irresistible and according to Angie it would have been rude to refuse.
Our next stop was the Poulnabrone dolmen, the best example in the country of a megalithic burial tomb and the kids were very impressed by the fact that when excavated in 1986 the remains of 30 people were found along with tools and jewellery that dated back to 2500 BC. According to local legend if a person runs around the Dolmen 10 times anti clockwise they will be blessed with the gift of fertility. Some of the kids did this so parents beware – they may need help with college fees for multiple kids!!!
Off we went again and this time to the town of Kilfenora, famous for the Kilfenors Céilí Band and seafood chowder in Vaughn’s pub. We had lunch there then were on our travels again – this time to the Cliffs of Moher, En route we passed through the town of Lisdoonvarna, which is renowned as a spa town but more importantly for the matchmaking festival that takes place in September and attracts thousands of visitors each year who are looking for an Irish husband or wife. The girls have assured us that when they are older this is definitely one festival they plan on attending – they’ll need a rich husband to look after all those kids they’re going to have after the fertility ritual at the dolmen…..
As we drove towards the Cliffs of Moher we turned a corner on the road and suddenly the cliffs appeared before us and it was absolutely breathtaking. These are the most visited attraction in Ireland, stretching down towards the Atlantic for almost 200 metres. As the saying goes “next stop America”. We also visited O’Brien’s Tower and the legend here is if you lay your hands and forehead on the Tower for 20 seconds you will be blessed with the gift of wealth- pretty handy don’t you think if you have been blessed with fertility after visiting the Dolmen and have a load of kids who plan to go to college???
Taryn took some fantastic photos and Anica bought another beautiful necklace which may be even nicer than the one she bought in Dublin!
And so we were on our way again, this time for a drive through Doolin, a lovely little town which has a reputation for fantastic traditional music and craic. On the way there we had a fantastic view of the Atlantic Ocean and Aran Islands, where we are heading tomorrow and took the coastal route home.
When we arrived back in Galway the kids had free time to explore Galway City but the kids opted to hang out on campus and have dinner parties. It was so cute to see them cooking and dressing for dinner. Staff visited the kids and had tea in their apartments and we also had two visitors – Dan’s wife Gill and sister Trish. They came armed with cake and ice cream so we were very glad to see them – especially Angie who hadn’t eaten chocolate in 5 hours. Liam also returned from his day with his family and said he had such a brilliant time.
“I had an awesome day – the Cliffs of Moher were so cool and when we turned the corner and saw them for the first time I just thought WOW. I’m excited for the Galway part of the tour”
And so ended another day with the excitement building for the trip to the Aran Islands tomorrow.

title: Protected: Leprechaun Crossing
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
It was with great relief that we saw the whole group assembled for breakfast in the dining room of the Killarney Court Hotel.  Those students who had been on the Ghost Tour of Killarney last night were still pretty shook this morning.  A hearty full Irish breakfast-the type that keeps cardiologists in Ferraris, soon had everyone feeling nice and perky and ready for the day ahead.
We left Killarney in a light drizzle for our Mini-Ring of Kerry bus tour, with our very own Brian Farrell of Burren Coaches.  First stop was the lovely little village of Kenmare.  Unfortunately, we had missed the organic food festival by a day, but the coffee and cakes were still delightful.  The highlight of the stop was the Neolithic Stone Circle.  This is an ancient burial site aligned with the rising sun.  Continuing the gory theme from last night, the altar in the middle of the circle is believed to have been the site of ritual slaughters of animals and possible even humans!  Amy was lucky enough to escape from our clutches this time.  Brian led us in an ancient Irish natural cleansing ceremony at the stones and we bestowed natural names on each other-as is the tradition in Kenmare.  Morgan was happy to be called “Red Oak” as with Brigid with “Buttercup,” but Rosie felt that her new name “Granola” didn’t capture the full essence of her enlightened aura.
From Kenmare, Brian took us on one of the most scenic drives in the country–over Moll’s Gap and Lady’s View.  The students took lots of photographs against the backdrop of Carauntoohill-Ireland’s highest mountain.  It was views such as this that established the Killarney area as the first tourist resort in Ireland-a reputation which has only been enhanced over the years. 
The descent from Lady’s view was spectacular, as we kept a close eye on the passing red deer.  Fortunately, Brian was alert enough to jam on the brakes before the Leprechaun Crossing and we proceeded to Torc Waterfall thankful for our lucky escape.  Through a gap in the trees at the beautiful Torc Waterfall, we spotted an unusual bright yellow disc in the sky.  A strange heat seemed to be emanating from it.  Mar and Raquel were delighted to inform us that they have something similar to this in Spain.  Apparently it is called “The Sun,” but none of the Irish ILE Staff were familiar with it.  Ha!
Today’s lunch stop was in the gorgeous grounds of Muckross Park.  In 1932 this became the first place in Ireland to be designated as a National Park and over the years the area covered by the park was expanded to become the Killarney National Park, which today covers over 15,000 acres.  Most of the students enjoyed the healthy sandwiches that they had picked up earlier, but some couldn’t resist the fancy cakes and buns in the café.
Our final stop was the ruins of Ross Castle over-looking Lough Leane.  This Castle was in partial ruins after Cromwell’s forces bombarded it in the 17th century, but enough of it remains for the students to have great fun climbing the walls and jumpng around the edge of the lake.  From there it was just a short bus ride past the most beautiful race course in the world back to town.  There the studnets enjoyed free time to sample some of the many restaurants, movies and amusement rides.  By the time everyone got back to the hotel in the evening, most of us were absolutely knackered and ready for bed before tomorrow’s long drive.
No leprechauns were harmed in the writing of this post.

title: Protected: A Bunch of Blarney
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
On Saturday, our very own Brian Farrell, from Burren Coaches, picked us up around 10:00 AM.  It was goodbye Dublin-hello Killarney.  
En route, students were treated to music from their very own playlist.  Each student added one song, to make a spectacular 2012 ILE Playlist.  Casey made sure she added a few from One Direction-her favorite band.  
Our first stop was Blarney Castle, where students were able to eat lunch and climb the narrow castle steps to kiss the Blarney Stone.  A few of the ILE Staff agreed that not everyone needed the Gift of the Gab, as many of our students already could talk their way out of any situation.  Ha!  There were some students that decided not to kiss the Blarney Stone, as they had hear rumors about what locals do to the stone at night.  Mums the word.  Ann said it was an experience, but she was a little nervous of the height.  
When many of the students had finished the adventure, they returned to the great Blarney Woolen Mills and purchased a few souvenirs-not to mention 99’s for the road.  Scones had coffee with Mr. and Mrs. Scones, so a lot of the students were excited to meet Scones’ parents.  They are great and maybe next year they will be able to come on tour with us.  Ha!  
Then it was time to get on the road again for another hour and a half-before Killarney.  An intense game of Dog/Tractor occurred, where Tyler got pretty competitive with Dan.  
After a long day of traveling, we eventually made it to the Killarney Court with Carrantoohill as the backdrop.  Students were given a stipend for dinner and had a chance to wander around the delightful picturesque town.  
Around 9:00 PM, the Michael Collins group of Kelly, James, Mariah, Rachel, Zach-with additions of Anica and Luis-were treated to the Killarney Ghost Tour.  For about two hours, students were told scary stories and shown places around Killarney that made the hair on your backs stand straight up.  Angie and Taryn had a few frights and let out some screams, as there were crazy things that kept touching their feet on the bus.  Ghosts, maybe.  A few of the students also took pictures in a local abbey and captured orbs.  Spooky!  What a laugh we had-great craic.  Luis said he had a blast and wanted to do it all over again.  
The night ended and all of the students were tucked away in their comfortable rooms at the hotel-excited for a fry the next morning.  Angie said that Taryn had some nightmares though-maybe do to all of the haunting escapades on the Ghost Tour.  Who knows.

title: Protected: Dublin Day and Music Workshop
author: tharrison
content_raw:
After such an exciting day yesterday, we decided to have a sleep in and organized breakfast for 8:45 AM instead of 8:30 AM!  That extra 15 minutes sure made a difference.
After a hearty breakfast, which met all our nutritional needs for the day, off everyone trundled to get our bus armed with packed lunches and battery-charged cameras to spend the day in Dublin-Ireland’s capital city and home of the second best Gaelic football team in the country.  Angie in her deluded state believes the best is County Antrim. 
Dublin Facts:
Home of the second best Gaelic Football Team, home of the current European Rugby Champions, home of the President of Ireland, home of the US Ambassador and owner of the Pittsburgh Steelers, home to Guinness and finally, and most importantly, home of Dan.
When we arrived in Dublin city, Kevin went with James and Zach to see the Book of Kells- which is kept in the 18th Century Old Library in Trinity College.  “The artwork of the Book of Kells is absolutely amazing,” said Zach.  
Also in the Old Library in Trinity College is the famous Long Room, which dates back to 1712 and stocks four million titles and showcases a 14th Century harp and a rare original printing of the 1916 Proclamation of the Irish Republic, made on Easter Sunday in Dublin’s Liberty Hall.  “The long room was awesome-it reminded me of where they eat dinner in the Harry Potter movies,” said James.  
Some of the kids also visited the National Art Gallery, where works by Van Gogh were being exhibited and others went to the National History Museum.
The kids also took a stroll to the famous Temple Bar area, which is buzzing with really cool cafes, clothing shops, and also houses the Irish Film Centre and U2’s recording studios.
Some kids just went shopping-a favorite hobby of Angie and she was delighted and excited to raid their bags to find out what they had bought when they got back on the bus!
Grafton Street, the best shopping area in Dublin, was where most of the kids spent the day after they had eaten lunch in the beautiful Stephen’s Green Park or had a feast of Thai food.  It was great as the summer sales were on, so a lot of the kids picked up bargains to bring home as presents.  The most popular shop was Carroll’s, which specializes in all things Irish-from tin whistles to really silly socks and hats.  Taryn picked up a pair of shamrock socks and a funny Irish hat-Angie told her she would put up with the hat, but no way was she walking on Grafton Street with Taryn wearing knee length shamrock socks.  Anica bought the most beautiful necklace with a shamrock made of green jewels in Carroll’s and the staff agreed that it is one of the nicest pieces of Irish jewelery that they have seen on the trip.  The bus came to pick everyone up at 3:45 PM and when we arrived back at Kings Hospital School all the kids trotted off to pack their newly acquired goods.
At 6:00 PM, Our Tom, Angie’s younger brother (Although he looks much older!), arrived with Our Ryan, Paddy, Máire and Brian from Belfast to do a traditional Irish music workshop with the kids. They brought with them a variety of instruments including a banjo, uileann pipes, and a bazouki. 
Before the workshop, the musicians got to meet and know the kids when we had a barbeque, as a celebration of our last night in Dublin.  Brian Farrell-owner of Burren Coaches and a great friend of the ILE, who drives us every year in Galway-was also there to meet the kids before the transfer to Killarney on Sunday.  He brought along his wife Ellie and kids and commented on what a fantastic group of kids we have this year. 
When we had eaten until we were ready to burst, the music workshop began.  The music was absolutely brilliant and the kids had a wonderful time listening to music being played by Irish Champion and world class musicians, who also told the kids about the history of the instruments they were playing.  The kids also had a chance to sing while the musicians played, with songs from Anica, Rachel and Brigid.  Petey also played guitar and Our Ryan, an Irish Champion guitar player, said that he was incredibly talented-go Petey!  While the music played, we were also treated to dancing by Mariah, Morgan and Mary Kate who were delighted by the chance to dance to live Irish music.  “I loved hearing real Irish music and learning about the instruments,” said Liam.
When the music ended, the kids rushed to get their glad rags on for the Saturday Night Disco-the last chance to say goodbye to all the kids they had met during their stay in Kings Hospital.  Ahhh!
All the kids returned to the dorms and finished packing before leaving for Killarney the following day.  Angie sang lullabies to the girls at bedcheck and tried not to upset them too much with a rendition of Paul’s Little Hen.  Angie thought it was a sad song until she realized the girls weren’t crying, but rather they were trying very hard to stifle laughter.  She is still trying to work out whether they were laughing at the lyrics or her singing.
And so concluded the final day of our stay in Dublin and with a final goodnight, lights were switched off for the last time in King’s Hospital.

title: Protected: Croker, Aras, and Drama-Perfect Day!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
On Friday, we had a full day in store!  Students first visited Croke Park for a tour, where they were able to watch the Leinster Semi Final for Gaelic Football our first week in Ireland.  Boy, time flies when you are having fun.  
Our tour began with a short video capturing the game day energy at the stadium.  Ryan said it was impressive.  Next, we took a behind the scenes tour, which led us through the day of an athlete on game day.  We got to see a locker room and hold county jersey’s up to our chests, walk through the last practice field athletes are on before stepping onto the field, and finally we were out in the stadium.  Once we were out in the stadium, several students began pointing to where our seats had been when we watched the game.  Brigid said she really appreciated the tour more now, after having witnessed a game there a few weeks ago.  The last two stops on our tour were the celebration room for athletes after a game and a box office that would be leased for $1,000 a year.  Ann said she was most amazed by the chandelier hanging in the banquet room.  It was made of Waterford Crystal and had 32 Gaelic Footballs hanging-representing the 32 counties of Ireland-along with 70 sliotars-representing the 70 minutes in a hurling game.  And…, when a county wins an All-Ireland Final, it will change to the color of the county.  So, when Dublin won last year, the lights were dark and light blue.  UP THE DUBS!
A day in the life of the ILE would not be complete without coffee, so before the President’s House, we made a coffee stop at the café in the Croke Park Museum.
We left Croke Park and drove to Phoenix Park for lunch.  Complete with chicken and stuffing sandwiches and popcorn.  This park has a unique landmark from a Papal visit to Ireland in 1979.  A large cross was erected in the park for this Mass that was attended by nearly 1.5 million people.  
When we had finished lunch, we continued driving through Phoenix Park, past the American Ambassador to Ireland’s residence, and onto the grounds of the President’s House-Áras an Uachtaráin.  As we drove up the driveway, there were several trees planted that had name plates.  These are trees that have been plated by visitors-such as queens, presidents of other countries, and other note worthy visitors.  Once at the house, we were welcomed at the entrance and invited in for tea and biscuits.  What an amazing experience that was!  Liam remarked, “I’m having tea at the president of Ireland’s house!  This is so coolest thing ever!  My mom would be so jealous!”  He surely enjoyed every minute of his visit.  Unfortunately, the President-Michael D. Higgins-was not at the Áras, so we weren’t able to meet him.  However, we were just happy to be welcomed into his home.  After tea, we were escorted through four beautiful rooms.  We saw the ball room, the dining room, a meeting room, and a greeting room.  In the greeting room was a Steinway piano and several of the students took a minute or two to tinkle the ivories-and the keys were even real ivory.  Anica, Liam, and Ryan all dazzled us with their abilities.  As we were exiting the Áras, we spotted Michael D.’s Bernese Mountain dogs.  All of the students went running over to pet the adorable dogs through the gate and take some pictures of their new friends.  
When we left the President’s House, we made one stop to pick a visitor who would join us for the night, David, Amy’s brother.  He was greeted with a traditional family call, which all of the students learned and performed marvelously.   
In the evening, we had our drama presentations.  Wahoo!  Michael Collins ended up being the winner and our guest judge, David, said they did a phenomenal job.  Their group won a ghost tour in Killarney.  Happy Days!  
For the remainder of the night, students enjoyed free time socializing with the other groups, watching movies, swimming, and relaxing.

title: Protected: Riverdance
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
As today was the last day of classes, I’m fairly confident the students were quite upset and in a state of mourning, but unfortunately that’s how the schedule was made out and we couldn’t change it.
Like normal, the classes for the students started at 9:00 AM and they began with Irish literature.  Angie taught the students about Patrick Kavanagh, the famous Irish author and the different works he completed. Kelly said she couldn’t wait to read more from Kavanagh.  Angie also gave the students a reading list of well known Irish authors-it’s not just the friendship and memories that outlive the duration of the ILE program, but also the passion for the Irish culture, language, and literature.
The students went straight into their Irish history class.  Although at this stage from the films and tours we expect all of them to be experts on the 1916 Rising and the Civil War-they did study it in class today.  This war is probably one of the most important turning points in modern Irish history.  In the Civil War, after the 1916 Rising, it was Michael Collins on the pro-treaty side fighting for a free state and Eamonn De Valera on the anti treaty side hoping to continue fighting the Brits until Ireland had a 32 county Republic.  Brigid and Lottie claimed they like De Valera, because in the film he was played by the actor that played prof. Snape in Harry Potter, but Kelly preferred Michael Collins because Liam Neeson was cute-not quite what we were looking for, but Kelly also said from her studies she liked Michael Collins as a person and believed in what he stood up for.
After this class it was time for the students to do their presentations on an Irish American of their choice.  This year we had a record number of students who chose to keep this project personal and research a member of their own family who came directly from Ireland.  Mary Kate was chosen to have the best presentation, where she spoke about her uncle.  Mary Kate really admires her uncle and her pride in him shone through in her presentation.  Ann and Petey gave very touching speeches about their grandparents.  
It came time for their Irish studies class, where each student was quizzed on the geography of Ireland-this is where Anica’s useful stories about their location came in handy.  She even got 100%!  Wowzers!
Finally, their last class.  The students learned one last lot of vocabulary-the Irish for hand (lamh:  laaawv), for foot (cos:  cuhss), for right (deis:  desh), for left (cle: klay) and for blue, green, yellow and red (gorm:  grr-um, glas:  gloss, bui:  bweee and dearg:  ja-rug).  This was when things got interesting, the Twister board came out.  The class was divided into teams of four or five and one winner made it through to the final from each team. The winner, was obviously Mariah, which was an easy guess due to her grace and balance she has learned from ballet classes.
After lunch there was a Celtic Frames Workshop set up for the students.  Each student was provided with the equipment needed and examples of Celtic designs and could decorate the frames as they wished.  When provided with the exact same supplies, it’s always fabulous to see how each student will make their frames turn out so differently.  Liam,  for example chose bright colors and decorated his frame by saying ILE 2012 along the bottom, whereas Ryan decided to do a Celtic design along the edge of his frame and leave the outside of the design wooden.  Both so different, but beautiful.
As the evening schedule was to be slightly different, this evening drama took place before dinner.  This was also to be the last practice for drama class, so dance was cancelled and drama was extended to a full hour.  While one group is keeping their drama top secret, (Ann Brigid, Conor, Kathleen, Lottie, and Tyler-we’re going to find out at some stage!), there’s another group that has an outline and a plan of improvisation, (Casey Luis, Mary Kate, Raquel, and Rosie).  All we’ll say is we can’t wait!
After dinner, there wasn’t much time to prepare, but the students managed to doll themselves up to the last just in time for the bus to collect everybody for Riverdance. Even though Morgan had seen it a few times already, she was  still excited to get to see it where it first began.  She said it was simply brilliant and she even thought it was better than the three times she had seen it previously.  Even our counselor Amy could barely contain her excitement-(scratch that, our counselor Amy can never contain her excitement!).  Brigid just LOVED it, and to be fair Liam was just a bit speechless after it.  The night ended with an entertaining bus ride home from Peter-at King’s Hospital.  He tried to see just how many times we could go around a round about.  What a perfect day!

title: Protected: Call Me Maybe
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
After an incredible day yesterday, Wednesday was a little slower and calmer class day.  Students were up around 8:30 AM for breakfast followed by class at 9:00 AM.  Today students learned about more James Joyce and Seamus Heaney in Angie’s Irish literature class.  While Dan taught the students about Daniel O’Connell and Charles Stewart Parnell in Irish history and about the Famine in Irish American history.  Taryn than finished up her slang class, which led into genealogy.  Zach enjoyed seeing his family crest and found it worthwhile learning about how to research his roots in Ireland.  The last class of the day was Dan’s Gaelic, which students played Bingo-from all of the numbers they had learned the day before.  It took a while for a winner, but Ann was successful.  She had to read her Bingo numbers back to Dan, so she is now a professional counting in Irish.  She won the book-PS I Love You and a Cork flag for her hard earned efforts.  Happy Days.  
The afternoon was jam packed full of workshops.  Amy did her two superb workshops, where students made Celtic designs on T-Shirts and made friendship bracelets in the colors of the Irish flag/Tri-Color.  Green representing the Catholics, Orange representing the Protestants, and white representing the peace between the two.  We were also fortunate enough to have our dear ILE friend, Corinna O’Donoghue visit us for the afternoon.  Corinna worked with the program as a teacher for four years-teaching Gaelic, Irish dance, and tin whistle.  We truly miss her.  She recently became engaged and we are all so happy for her.  So, we were lucky enough to have her back for a day, as she taught Mary Kate and Morgan a very challenging Irish dance routine from her Irish championship dancing days.  She was very impressed with their abilities and said they were both naturals-destined for Riverdance.  
Later in the night, after dinner, students had drama and dance.  In drama, students finished working on their plays that they will perform on Friday night.  In dance, students learned the second part of the Eight Hand Reel.  Then we had a half hour break before the long awaited talent show.  Highlights of the talent show were Anica singing and playing guitar with Mariah dancing, Rachel singing, Petey playing the guitar, Morgan and Mary Kate Irish dancing, and a few special numbers by the beloved staff.  Raquel said her favorite was the ILE Staff’s skit-where Kevin was hilarious.  Each drama group also prepared a short act for the talent show.  When the talent show was finished, Angie sang everyone a lullaby and then everyone was ready to dance the night away at the disco.  Bring on Call Me Maybe-shout out to you Scott McIver!

title: Protected: A Giant of a Day
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
We had an early start this morning-6:00 AM, but the King’s Hospital kitchen staff pulled out all the stops with Cheerio’s for breakfast.  We all enjoyed the meal in silence, before hopping on the bus for the long journey north.
First stop when we got over the border was the brand spanking new Titanic Exhibition in Belfast Docks.  This center was only opened in April to commemorate the 100th Anniversary of the ship’s maiden voyage.  The exhibition exceeded all expectations.  The highlight of the trip was probably a cool cable car style ride down into a recreation of the construction of the hull of the ship.  There were loads more great features inside and fortunately there was plenty of Kleenex on stand-by for those students who were devastated by the unexpected sad ending.
Angie was kind enough to point out her summer house to us as we traveled north to the Causeway Coast.  Unfortunately, we don’t have any pictures of Belfast Castle.:)  The bus passed through Bushmills in Co. Antrim, home of the oldest legal distillery in the world, but time constraints meant we couldn’t stop to sample the fare.  Unfortunately, we had similar time constraints when we passed the Jameson Distillery in Midleton last week. I guess everyone will just have to come back to Ireland in a few years time when they are of age.
After a delicious and nutritious lunch on the grass roof of the brand new Giant’s Causeway Interpretive Center, the group were ready for what is always one of the highlights of the entire trip-the Giant’s Causeway.  All the students, at least those who paid attention in Dan’s Irish history class, knew that the Giant’s Causeway was built by a Scottish giant called Benandonner, so that he could attack the Irish Giant Fionn McCool.  When Fionn saw Benandonner approaching he was terrified by the size of his Scottish opponent, so he ran and hid in his house.  Fionn’s wife dressed Fionn up as a baby and put him into their crib.  Benandonner took one look at this massive baby and said “My God, if this is the size of the baby, the father must be huge.”  With that, Benandonner ran back to Scotland tearing the Causeway up behind him as he went.  The students were smart enough to discount the childish rumours about the Causeway being made up by hexagonal basalt rocks, which were formed when molten lava cooled rapidly towards the end of the last Ice Age.  We also learned the valuable lesson that even rockslides can’t stop Tyler.
Everyone had great fun clambering all over the Causeway, the Giant’s Boot, and the Giant’s Organ.  Then it was time to move on to the Carrick-a-rede Rope Bridge.  This is a tiny little bridge made from rope and planks of wood which were thrown out to a tiny offshore island by salmon fishermen.  Now it features in most of the ads and brochures for Tourism Ireland, and with good reason.  All the students and most of the staff were brave enough to make it out to the island and the beautiful views were accentuated by one of the first sunny days we have had since the start of the tour.  But remember, the ILE motto-“There is no such thing as bad weather, just the wrong clothes!”
From Carrick-a-rede, we stopped at Ballycastle where the ice-cream was great and the tangerines were even better.  A long bus ride home beckoned, but we had One Direction to keep us company so the time just flew.  We were so tired by the time we got home that some of the girls were fast asleep before Angie got to sing her nightly lullaby. 
Amy and Kevin said it was their favorite day of the trip yet!

title: Protected: Away with the Fairies
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
On Monday, the students were well and truly settled into Dublin and began making friends with both Irish and Spanish students that are doing different summer camps in the same school.  Monday was a typical class day for the ILE students.  They had five full classes before lunch time.
Angie started by doing two literature classes with everybody.  In the first class, the students learned about the life of WB Yeats.  Casey did a quick recap of what she had learned and said that she was interested in the inspiration that Yeats used for his poetry-which was the rough landscape of where he was brought up.  The next class the students had was Irish American Studies with Taryn.  Since the students had been in the country for ten days now, Taryn felt it was necessary for them to know about the slang that was common in Ireland. Students were warned not to go home “Up the Duff” and were advised to steer clear of anybody that was “Away with the Fairies.”  Next, Angie came back in for her second literature class of the day.  In this class, the students learned all about Ulysses.  It worked well, as some students have mentioned they may be interested in visiting some locations-such as the bookstore that Leopold Bloom went to in this novel and they will have free time to do this in Dublin on Saturday.  Lottie left the class saying she found it interesting that there were no periods in one of his chapters!  Finally, Dan came in to teach the students how to count in Irish and numbers up as far as 100, (Cead-Kay-ud). Now fortunately for James, once he gets to Galway, not only can he introduce himself to all the Irish girls, but he can also give out his number.  This class was in preparation for an intense game of Bingo that has been planned for the next class day with Dan.  
After lunch, the students had three hours free time.  Jenni and Kathleen made use of the shopping center being so close to us and decided to buy some new clothes to look fabulous in for the next disco.  Thankfully there was a Starbucks close to the school, so many students were able to keep updated with parents, siblings, boyfriends, girlfriends and in some cases prospective girlfriends, but we won’t start naming names now!
In Kings Hospital where we are staying there is a recreational room with table tennis set up and Mar and Raquel are most likely going to be professionals by the end of the trip with the amount of table tennis they are playing.  Of course the boys have a television in their dorm, so a few boys spent some time studying the Irish accent through the TV, which I’m sure Anica, Anne and Rachel will be jealous of since they are trying to perfect their Irish accents before returning to the states.  Although Rachel seems to have arrived to Ireland with plenty of practice on her Irish accent so she has it almost nailed.
Everybody arrived back to the school in time for dinner and went straight into practicing their drama afterwards.  All the characters have been picked and the scripts written.  It is just practice and costumes that need to be completed.  From what little I’ve stolen a peek at, let’s just say these drama presentations will be interesting.  As usual, the students went straight into dance class, which they all love thanks to their amazing teacher Scones.  This time they were only doing the first half of a dance, because from past experience we concluded too many steps can not be comprehended in our 40 minute time slot.  The trouble was they would have to remember all these steps for the next dance class.  This should be fun.  The dance was the eight hand reel and is typically a more advanced dance class, but we felt the students we have this year were such naturals they could handle it.
After dance, Angie had organized a work shop for every student on Northern Ireland in preparation for our trip to Belfast and the Giants Causeway on Tuesday.  She gave the students details on the troubles that happened in Belfast in modern times and what life was like growing up in Belfast.  Since Angie had grown up right in the middle of Belfast in the 1970’s and 1980’s, she was almost too qualified to let everybody know what had happened.
It was early to bed tonight, as it was early to rise on Tuesday for our incredible northern tour.

title: Protected: Slainte!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
Today was jam packed full of excitement!  After breakfast, around 8:30 AM, we got on a bus and headed to Kilmainham Gaol.  This was a jail opened in 1796 and it is most famous for its imprisonment of captured revolutionaries and other political leaders of the time, although it also held captive several hundred children, women, and other men.   The prison closed its gates in 1924, when Eamon de Valera was the last prisoner to be released.  Eamon would later become Ireland’s Taoiseach and President.  
The tour was incredible.  There was an eeriness in being there as we stood in the prison cells, walked through the same halls that prisoners had walked, and stood in the courtyard where several had been executed.  Ryan said it was very powerful, while Kelly added that it tied everything together perfectly that they had learned in Dan’s Irish history class.  
After a solemn morning tour, we went to the Guinness Brewery for a tour.  The massive piece of land was leased by Arthur Guinness in 1759 when he signed a 9,000 year lease; he had great faith in the fate of his dream and rightly so.  The tour is a self-guided tour in the worlds largest pint glass which makes up the storehouse.  A person touring, travels up through four floors, as they watches how Guinness is brewed right before their eyes.  For those guests who are over 18, they may proceed to the next floor and learn how to pull the perfect pint of Guinness; there is quite a skill to be mastered in perfecting this art.  The next two floors have bars and pubs-serving Guinness of course.  The very top of the storehouse is called the Gravity Bar.  Guests over the age of 18 may enjoy a complimentary pint of Guinness here while enjoying a breathtaking 360-degree view of Dublin.  Since Petey, Rosie, and Tyler are over 18, they all were able to Pull the Perfect Pint, receive a certificate of completion, and have a wee sip of the stout.  Petey and Rosie said they thought the taste wasn’t bad, while Tyler thought it was disgusting.  Other students simply enjoyed learning about the beer that is so well known in Ireland.  Mar said she thought the views from the Gravity Bar were amazing.  After the tour, students stocked up on Guinness souvenirs for families and friends.  Slainte-meaning cheers in Irish!
Originally, the plan for today included a hike, but since it was lashing rain we decided against the hike and returned back to King’s Hospital with a little over an hour to spare until dinner time.  The bus made a drop off at Liffey Valley Shopping Center, where students had the choice to either hang out at the mall or head back to King’s Hospital, or in Ryan’s case go back to King’s Hospital-only to decide he really did want to go shopping with all of the money he had!  At 5:00 PM students checked back in and at 5:30  PM it was time for a delicious dinner.  After dinner, students had free time until 8:30 PM, when we watched the movie In the Name of the Father before we prepared to head north on Tuesday.

After lunch, Dan took us on a walking tour of Dublin.  We began walking down Dawson Street and passed several notable landmarks-including Trinity College-one of the oldest colleges in the world and Temple Bar-an area of Dublin’s city center housing trendy clubs, pubs, restaurants, and stores. There is a drama group, a sports camp, and an English language camp.  
The girls are staying in one dorm with five girls to one room and the boys are in a separate dorm with two boys to one room-both en suite.  After getting settled in the rooms, it was time for dinner.  The night ended with a disco, disco, disco. title: Our Week in Waterford
author: tharrison
content_raw:
This morning we had a little time to sleep in and have a later breakfast before we got on the bus around 9:30 am and headed off for Cahir Castle.  This castle was owned by the Butler family from 1375 – 1964 when it was sold to the Irish state after the last heir died.  Today it is a historical monument which is maintained by the Office of Public Works.  This castle was built to be undefeatable.  It was built on a rock foundation which made it nearly impossible for enemies to dig underground tunnels for attack purposes.  There is also a river that naturally splits to surround the castle on both sides.  If attackers got inside the first layer of castle walls, there were still several layers of defense which made it difficult for attackers to get to the inside walls.  The castle stood strong until heavy cannon balls entered into battle.  In 1599, the castle was taken under attack by Queen Elizabeth’s forces.    In 1647, the Butlers abandoned the castle to Oliver Cromwell.  After all of this, the Butler’s still maintained possession of the castle.  The Butler family did major restorations to the castle between the years 1840 and 1846.
While we were at Cahir, we were taken on a guided tour and then the students had a while to explore.  Students enjoyed the authentic feeling of being in a medieval castle.  There were cannons sitting in the inside court yard, cannon balls stuck in the side of the towers from battle, and old stone staircases.
Around noon we left Cahir Castle for Kilkenny Castle.  When we arrived we went and ate lunch on a beautiful green grass right outside the castle.  The weather even cooperated for us!  When we went on the tour it was much different than the tour at Cahir Castle.  This tour was mainly a self guided tour with tour guides spaced throughout the castle to share extra information.  Thank goodness we had Dan who filled in as our personal tour guide.
William the Earl Marshall was the first to begin building the castle and completed the construction in 1213. The original castle was square-shaped with 4 towers – one at each corner.  Today 3 of the original towers remain.
The Butler family bought the Castle in 1391 and lived there until 1935. They were Earls, Marquesses and Dukes of Ormonde. The property was given to Ireland in 1967 and is currently managed by the Office of Public Works.
We got back to Waterford just in time for dinner.  After dinner we had our evening activity.  What better way to celebrate the 2012 Summer Olympics than by having some Olympics of our own?  The kids had a variety of activities they had to complete with their assigned team including coming up with a team name and anthem for their team.  The weather was still in our favor during the Olympics and the rain began just as we were finishing.
For the remainder of the night students watched movies, played outside, and played cards and board games in the staff room.   After a long day, it was finally time for bed to rest up for the day ahead.

Over the course of the week, the ILE students were given an assignment to write a limerick (AABBA rhythm) on a historical literary or political figure   It was great to see how creative the students were, as many wrote some fantastic pieces. 
However, Mariah had the winning Limerick on Samuel Beckett.
Samuel Beckett threw some bit fits;

He felt this strong fire
For his native Eire,
Because it was controlled by darn Brits.

title: Protected: Rain, Rain-Go Away!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Tuesday July 3rd, we left for Cork at 8:30 AM. We headed to Kinsale to see Charles Fort.  With the early start there was almost complete silence on the bus down!  
Charles Fort is a classic example of a late 17th century star-shaped fort.  William Robinson, architect and Superintendent of Fortifications, is credited with designing the fort.  As one of the largest military installations in the Ireland, Charles Fort has been associated with some of the most momentous events in Irish history.  The most significant of these are the Williamite War 1689-1691 and the Civil War 1922-1923.  Charles Fort was declared a National Monument in 1973.  Across the estuary is James Fort designed by Paul Ive in 1602.  This combination of forts meant that the English had a very strong defense against any of their European enemies trying to attack through Ireland. 
Charles Fort is also associated with the battle of Kinsale in 1601-The Flight of the Earls, which saw the end of the old Gaelic aristocracy.  Ann and Brigid both agreed that they loved having the chance to explore the fort, but felt that the rain was a bit of a turn off.
Charles Fort is where a German submarine torpedoed a passenger ship “The  Lusitania,” off the Old Head of Kinsale as it was sailing from New York to England.  This was a major factor in the USA’s eventual entry into the war against Germany.
Kinsale is a very picturesque town on the coast.  Driving in you pass a collage of yachts on one side with buildings of all colors, shapes, and sizes on the other.  
Upon arriving at Charles Fort, we met with our tour guide, William.  Unfortunately, it was raining quite heavily, but we started our tour outside regardless.  William showed us a mosaic map embedded in the ground of the entire fort.  William told us about the standards of living for English army men that were living in Charles Fort, which we learned were not vey attractive at all.  However, they were in fact better than any other available options.  Many men retired from the army owing money, as they had to pay for accommodation, food and uniforms and were not paid well during their time. 
We ended the tour indoors thankfully, and left for lunch.  As per usual, it was still pouring from the heavens so we could not explore Kinsale.  Although, we managed to get a bit of shopping time in while in Cork City.  Shortly after all the gifts were bought for everybody back home:), we headed to Dungarvan in Co. Waterford for some food.  Kelly said she was so happy that the chicken actually tasted real for once!  Everybody was allowed to explore and choose where they wanted to eat for dinner before we arrived back to Newtown Boarding School for the evening.  James arrived back to the bus saying sweet, not necessarily because he liked the town, but because he was really enjoying all of the sweets or candy as we call it in the US!
Every student got a short break before they met in the classroom to perfect their limericks with Amy and Kevin for half an hour and then went straight into the dance class with Scones.  In dance, they learned their first Irish reel, “The Walls of Limerick,” which is a very famous dance that most Irish children learn at ceili’s.
Finally the weather improved and all of the kids spent the evening playing ball and practicing their newly learned Gaelic Football and Hurling skills before everybody got plenty of sleep in time to celebrate July 4th.

title: YOIIO-You’re Only in Ireland Once!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
On Tuesday, students had their second day of classes.  The morning began with a breakfast of bread, cereal, and fruit-followed by Dan’s Irish history class.  
In Dan’s class, they learned about Cú Chulainn, Fionn mac Cumhaill, Newgrange, and St. Patrick.  
In between Irish history and Irish studies, students were able to take a stroll down to the Waterford Crystal Factory and have a tour to see how the beautiful ornate crystal was made.  “From moulding, to blowing, to etching, to cutting-it was very interesting,” said Brigid.  A few students even bought some beautiful pieces for souvenirs for their parents.  Kathleen said she wanted her mom to know (on the ILE Blog) that she wanted to buy her something from the factory, but everything was too expensive:).    
Students returned to Taryn’s Irish studies class where they learned about the Geography and Geology of Ireland.  
The last class of the day was Gaelic, where students had a basic introduction to the language-along with how to say hello and how are you.  Dia dhuit and Conás átá tú.  
The afternoon was devoted to free-time in Waterford or two optional workshops-both led by our amazing ILE Counselor, Scones.  
The first workshop was Tin Whistle and Scones taught the students how to play, “My Heart Will Go On,” from the Titanic.  Scones said she was amazed by the musical ability of Anica and Conor.  They both picked up the tune very quickly.  James and Zach also did well.  Many perfected the tune throughout the day and a few have even bought tin whistles to learn more songs during the program.  The song was definitely stuck in the heads of many of the students throughout the day, as you heard them humming around campus.  
The next workshop was Scones, and it couldn’t have been more fitting than having OUR VERY OWN Scones teach the students how to bake these delicious Irish treats.  Nearly all of the students wanted to learn how to make Scones’ mother’s famous recipe.  It was a full house in the kitchen.  Scones said that there were some fantastic bakers in the group.  Ryan was an excellent kneader and Lottie’s crew said that they got more flour on their clothes than probably in the actual scones.  After the students had mixed the dough, added raisins, and rolled them into unique shapes, the kitchen ladies put them in the oven so they would be ready for our tea time.  
Needless to say, once tea time rolled around, everyone sampled the goodies and were impressed with how scrumptious they were.  A few drizzled butter and jam on them, while others just ate them plain.  A few of the girls said they couldn’t wait to make them at home for their families.  Casey said they were yummy! 
Tea time was followed by Amy’s Waterford Scavenger Hunt.  Students were split into teams and had to find specific items and take pictures throughout the town.

title: Protected: Up the Dubs!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Today started out with breakfast at 9:00 AM.  Students were all excited about the opportunity to have a lie-in.   After breakfast, they got on the bus and headed to Dublin to watch two Gaelic Football games at Croke Park.   The drive from Waterford to Dublin took about two hours, so most students took a little nap on the way.   When we got to Dublin, students ate lunches that they had packed back at Newtown Boarding School at a nearby park, called Mountjoy Square.  After lunch, we headed for Croke Park to watch the games.  
Croke Park is a sport’s stadium and is the principal stadium and headquarters of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA).  Since 1884, the site has been used primarily by the GAA to host Gaelic games, most notably the annual finals of the All-Ireland Senior Football Championship and Senior Hurling Championship.  
The walk to the game became more and more crowded with people the closer students got to the stadium.   Street vendors were selling flags, headbands, jackets, and scarves.   People were also beginning their celebrations at local pubs, so there was a great buzz.   Once we were inside the stadium, we were channelled into a river of people all moving different directions.   Students eventually found their seats in the Davin Stand with great views of the pitch.  Students were introduced to Kildare and Meath first in the Minor Match.  Meath was the winning team in this round, and it was a close game.  Then students had some time before the next battle, so they indulged in hamburgers, hot dogs, and Cadbury’s chocolate.  YUM!  Next, students were able to watch Dublin play Wexford.  For much of the game, Wexford was in the lead, but Dublin pulled through in the second half and came out victorious.  Ath Cliath 2-11 (17) to Loch Garman 1-10 (13).  Up the Dubs!  Since Dan is from Dublin, he was biting his nails and was nervous a few times throughout the match.  “It was amazing to see how enthusiatic the supporters were from different counties,” said Anica.  Rachel said it was a great atmosphere.  Brigid and Lottie purchased a Dublin jacket and a jersey, so they were thrilled to see Dublin won.  
Since students had learned how to play Gaelic Football on Saturday, they saw the combination of the American sports-basketball, football, soccer, and volleyball.  Dan said the objective of Gaelic Football was to bring the ball, which is similar in appearance to a volleyball, down to the opponent’s goal and score.  Players could carry the ball while running, but every four steps they must dribble the ball like a basketball or kick and catch the ball.  To pass the ball, players execute a move similar to an underhand serve in volleyball.  In order to score, a player may kick the ball in the air through posts that are similar to the goal posts in American football.  This will earn the team one point.  Players may also kick the ball on the ground into a net similar to an American soccer net.  Scoring this way will earn the team three points.  
After watching the matches, we headed to King’s Hospital for dinner.  When we travel to Dublin next Saturday, we will be staying in King’s Hospital.  Luis, Mar, and Raquel were eager to get back to Waterford to see Spain play Italy in soccer, so we ate dinner quickly and hopped back on the bus to Waterford.  The game began while we were enroute, so we listened to it on the radio on the way down to Waterford.  We arrived in Waterford to catch the last 10-15 minutes of the game.  In the end, Spain was victorious over Italy with a score of 4 to 0.  Go Spain!  Mar and Raquel taught us a few Spanish chants and were thrilled to see their team win.
When the game was over, we put a movie on for the students.  Some kids watched the movie, others hung out in the Staff Room playing cards, and several hung out in the music hall playing piano, guitar, and dancing.  Then bed time rolled around.  After such a long day, you would think they would be ready for bed right away, but several of the girls were still quite energized from eating too much candy (Cough, cough-Ann Keating:).  Around midnight,  the lights were off and the rooms were quiet with everyone resting up for the exciting day that tomorrow would bring.

title: Protected: Gaelic Football and Hurling-Wey Hey!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
Students woke up early Saturday morning after getting plenty of sleep the night before.  They felt refreshed and rejuvenated from their jet let and were excited to start their first day of class.  
For breakfast, they enjoyed brown bread, a variety of cereals, toast, and orange juice.  After getting some food into their stomachs, they delved into their first Irish literature class with Angie.  Angie shared the history of Irish literature with them and read a story by Frank O’Connor.  Rachel said it was very interesting.
Since the students were going to the Leinster Finals on Sunday, the Waterford GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association) came and gave an incredible Gaelic Football and Hurling Workshop to the students.  This threw off our schedule a little, but was well worth it.  Mid-morning was devoted to learning these two incredible Irish sports.  
Gaelic Football is a sport played between two teams of 15 players on a rectangular grass pitch.  The objective of the sport is to score points by passing the ball through the other team’s goals, a set of two upright posts separated by a crossbar 8.2 feet above the ground.
Hurling has prehistoric origins and has been played for at least 3,000 years.  It is thought to be the world’s fastest field team game in terms of game play.  One of Ireland’s native Gaelic games, it shares a number of features with Gaelic Football, such as the field and goals, number of players, and much terminology.  There is a similar game for women called Camogie.  
ILE’s Friend and Waterford GAA Coach, Mark Cooney, first taught the students Hurling.  He showed them what a hurley and sliotar were and then ran some important drills with them to get them comfortable with the sport.  He said that Conor, Luis,  and Tyler were naturals at the game.  They had some fantastic hand-eye coordination.  Anica and Casey also had some great plays.  After learning the basics, the students had a little friendly competition with each other.  It was fun to watch.  “I like the way they pass it up and down the pitch,” said Casey.
The students eventually switched over to Gaelic Football, which they were all looking forward to, since they would see a game at Croke Park on Sunday.  Again, Mark demonstrated the important techniques and ran some drills.  He decided to make a challenge for two teams to see who could hand pass the ball and kick it over the goal post the most.  The deal-the losing team would have to buy the winning team McFlurry’s from McDonalds.  It was close, but with Luis’ stellar soccer skills, his team was able to pull off the win!  Mark told the students that he was extremely impressed with their talents and said they were the best group he has ever worked with from the Irish Life Experience.  Props to the 2012 ILE’ers!
After getting a great workout, the students had built up quite an appetite.  They raced over to the cafeteria for a hard earned dinner.  The students then had free time to explore Waterford.  Dan brought a group in and gave them a quick tour.  Many of them exchanged money and bought a few necessities, while others just wandered and soaked it all in.  Brigid said she really likes the town and it’s a nice size.  
When students returned back to Newtown Boarding School, they enjoyed a nice meal of lasagne.  After tea, they had their first drama and dance class.  They started working on their limericks in drama class and Scones taught them the basic 3’s and 7’s of Irish dance.  Morgan, our Irish dancing student, even demonstrated a jig for the students.  It was impressive to see.  
Many of the students decided to watch Old School and some of them just hung out in the Music Hall.  Liam said it was a great day and the perfect beginning to the ILE!

title: Protected: Welcome to Waterford
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
After students had arrived Dublin Airport on Friday, met Mar and Raquel-from Spain, they began their three hour bus journey south to Waterford.  The students were definitely jet legged, so many were able to catch some much needed shut eye.  To break the drive down to Waterford, we stopped at Glendalough, so the students could stretch their legs and enjoy a packed lunch of apples, crisps, sandwiches, and sweets.  
Glendalough, or the Glen of Two Lakes, is one of the most important sites of monastic ruins in Ireland.  It is also known as the City of the Seven Churches.  Fourteen centuries have passed since the death of its founder, St. Kevin, when the valley was part of Ireland’s Golden Age.  
The two lakes, which gave the valley its name, came into existence thousands of years ago, after the Ice Age, when great deposits of earth and stone were strewn across the valley in the area where the Round Tower now exists.  The mountain streams eventually formed a large lake.  The Pollanass River spread alluvial deposits across the center of the lake and created a divide to form the Upper and Lower Lakes.  The Glenealo River flows in from the west into the Upper Lake, which is the larger and deepest of the two lakes.
Before the arrival of St. Kevin this valley would have been desolate and remote.  It must have been ideal for St. Kevin as a retreat and area to be away from it all.  St. Kevin died in 617 AD at the age of 120 years and his name and life’s work is forever entwined with the ruins and the Glendalough Valley.  Our amazing ILE Counselor, Kevin, was also thrilled to learn his name was so well associated with Glendalough.  “This is awesome,” he said.  
After our packed lunch, Dan gave the students a tour of the Round Tower, the cemetery filled with beautiful Celtic crosses, St. Kevin’s Church and took them on a short walk along the Lower Lake.  Jenni, from Montana said is was beautiful.  Ann said she enjoyed the fresh air after being on the plane the day before.  
When we had finished our short break at Glendalough, we hopped back on the bus to finish our trip to Newtown Boarding School in Waterford.  Once we arrived Newtown Boarding School, students were able to get settled in their rooms.  We had tea afterwards, followed by a brief orientation.  Students were then able to deposit their money and passports into the ILE Bank, before we had a few evening activities.  Amy, Kevin, and Scones led the group in some ice-breakers of the Human Knot and Lover’s Leap.  Many of the students were very exhausted after the past few days, so it was early to bed, early to rise.  Conor said that the past few days were a good bonding experience for everyone and he was looking forward to what the rest of the experience had in store for him.

title: Protected: The Summer of a Lifetime Begins
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
Just a quick update on our long travel day to Ireland.  Thursday, the 28th, marked the departure of the 2012 Irish Life Experience.  The day began around 10:30 AM, when Ryan, from Minnesota arrived.  Shortly thereafter, a few more students started trickling in from California, Florida, Illinois, Michigan, and Montana.  Since our Aer Lingus flight was delayed until 11:00 PM, students had plenty of time for introductions and to explore and become familiar with Terminal 4 at JFK International Airport.  A few of them listened to their iPods, played card games, and read their books.  Many of them checked out Duty Free and got any last minute essentials they might have forgotten to pack.  They also got their fill on the American comfort food of Kentucky Fried Chicken, McDonald’s, and S’Barro, before they would enjoy the delicious Irish cuisine…, of potatoes:).
Amy-one of our wonderful ILE Counselors-said it was a very long day, but ran smoothly.  In fact, it was probably the easiest departure day we have ever had from JFK in the history of the ILE, with all of the students on connecting flights arriving by 7:00 PM. Wey hey!
Local students and families started to arrive around 5:00-6:00 PM.  They were met by Amy, Kevin, and Taryn, where they signed-in with the Irish Life Experience, received their T-Shirts and Tourism Ireland goodies.  We eventually were allowed to check-in with Aer Lingus and before we knew it, it was time to go through Security and board our plane to the Emerald Isle.  Parents asked last minute questions and said their final good-byes, before we were able to capture a picture of the group.  A few tears were shed and students were filled with a lot of excitement and nervousness about the adventure they were to embark upon. 
We breezed through Security and boarded EI 108, direct to Dublin.  The ILE occupied the middle of the plane, got settled in their seats, and relaxed with a great selection of movies for the six hour journey across the pond.  We even sang Happy Birthday to Rosie, from Montana, as she celebrated her 18th Birthday traveling from Montana.  Students were exhausted from their travel day, so quite a few of them got some much needed shut eye.  
Tyler said his favorite part of the day was flying into Ireland and noticing all of the different shades of green.  We finally arrived Dublin Airport around 11:00 AM on Saturday morning.  
We then proceeded to collect our luggage and were happy to find out that no bags were lost in the process.  We exited the terminal and were greeted with warm welcomes from Angie, Dan, and Scones.  We also met our newsest addtions, Mar and Raquel, from Spain-along with their leaders from Go Inspired, Margo and Manuel.  It was an overwhelming day, but we are all happy to be in Ireland!  “It’s a small world and we need to see all of it,” said Petey from DC.  Liam, from Massachusetts, said it’s nice to be home.

title: Olympic Hopeful-Melinda Owen
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Melinda Owen, from my hometown of Polson, Montana will be competing in the Olympic Trials for pole vaulting today at 5:30 PM and on Sunday at 2:30 PM (Pacific Time).  Please send her good vibes and cheer her on.  
“I have always been pulled toward sports.  I think it was because of my family dynamics. My father used to wake my siblings and me up in the morning after he got back from his run, and we all did sit-ups and push-ups together.  When we all finished, we got to sit on his back while he did his.  He made it very fun for us.  We were in clubs depending on the number of sit-ups and push-ups we could do, and we always were trying to get in the next club!  Because of this, we all loved being both active and competitive!  And both of my parents were very supportive with any and every sport we wanted to try.  I did pretty much everything that Polson had to offer, so when it came time in high school to make a decision on just three, it was very tough.  Track, and specifically pole vault, was difficult to spend much time on due to the fact that it typically snows off and on until June in Montana.  This is why I felt it was so important I participated in both basketball and volleyball as well.  With the combination of the three sports, I believed that helped make me a more well rounded athlete.
The journey that I have taken to get me where I am today has been nothing less than amazing.  The people around me were willing to make sacrifices for me, because of the work ethic my parents had instilled in me.  My high school coach stuck around even after all his kids had graduated to see me to my own state championship title!  In college I was fortunate enough to have a coach that selflessly worked harder than any other person I have yet met in my 25 years.  The time he dedicated to my training was a large part in what helped me become the best collegiate vaulter by my senior year.  Because of that mark, I was then asked by the Olympic coach, Ty Sevin, to join his small group of athletes at the Arco Olympic Training Center in Chula Vista, California.  So as you can see, there really isn’t one person or situation that got me where I am, but instead it was a combination of very dedicated people and some rare opportunities.  My most stable help has and always will come from my faith and family. Their combination keeps me humble, honest, passionate and loved.  Without all of it I would have never became the person I am today.”
GOOD LUCK, MELINDA!!!

title: More Helpful Advice from ILE 2011 Alumnae, Fiona Tomlin
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hey!  I’m back! 
Although Ryan did a superbly thorough job of filling you guys in on some ILE essentials, I would like to add a few things. (From a girl’s perspective.)
Fiona’s ILE Survival Guide for Girls:
1.  Bring a small bag that is easy to carry around that fits your wallet, a digital camera, an international phone if you have one-not necessary, and maybe some lip balm or gum.  Leave the heftier tote bags at home.  Even if it’s new and adorable and fits all your necessities.  Trust me, most of those things aren’t remotely necessary. 
2.  Get an international phone if you plan on updating your family by phone, but you can just as easily do without one if you don’t think you’ll need it.  I don’t recommend using your time in cities relying on Internet Cafes to E-mail/Facebook family and friends. If you want one, there are international phones and plans that let you add minutes for really cheap. (Go to Vodaphone.)
3.  Your beloved curling iron/hair straightener can still blow out even with a proper electrical adapter.  This can result in burning your hair off, leaving a weird short spot in the back of your blonde tresses.  (Neither confirming nor denying if this tip is related to a personal anecdote.)  Basically, bring one if you can’t live without it, but use sparingly and carefully.
4.  You’re given a lot of independence on the trip, but also the right amount of supervision.  Don’t abuse your independence.  Listen to directions and stay within the kind boundaries set forth by your wonderful counselors and you will have no problems.
5.  This might be painfully girly, but here it goes:  Buy a new perfume before you leave the US, (Travel size so TSA can’t freak out.) and use it daily in Ireland.  Science shows us that smell is the most sharply tuned sensory association tool we have.  In other words, when you’re back stateside and missing the ILE or your ILE friends, one whiff will take you right back to the Emerald Isle.   I’m so glad I did this even if you’re laughing at me right now for spritzing perfume in a cloud around my laptop as I write this.  Memories.
6.  Bring comfortable, broken in flats or sneakers that go with everything.  You do a lot of walking and you don’t want to attempt to break in new shoes no matter how cute you think they’ll look on the cobblestones of Temple Bar. Blisters are never cute.  Also bring a lightweight raincoat and rain boots for wet days, of which there’s a good amount.
7.  Ryan touched on this but…, take pictures!  However, don’t take too many pictures.  Don’t focus on simply snapping away!  Look around, relish the moment, IN the moment, then snap away.  Take meaningful photos of things that you love or inspire you.  And most importantly, hand someone else the camera once in awhile.  What’s a hundred beautiful green landscape shots if your beautiful self isn’t even in one of them?!
8.  Connect with any Irish family you may have and see if you can arrange to meet up with them for one day or just dinner.  I did this.  I know Ryan did too and it is a fantastic new way to experience your heritage.  The ILE Program is very accommodating when helping you meet up with your family, but be sure to arrange it well in advance.
9.  Buy an Aran Knit Sweater from the Aran Islands.  You’ll thank me when you’re back at home, cuddled up in it with a cup of tea and doused in your “memory-perfume,” daydreaming about your summer in Ireland.
10.  HAVE FUN! 
Love, 
Fiona Tomlin-San Diego, CA-ILE 2011

title: Helpful Advice from ILE 2011 Alumnae, Fiona Tomlin
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hi 2012 ILE’ers! 
I’m Fiona Tomlin, an ILE 2011 Alumnae from San Diego.  Let me first of all congratulate you on your acceptance to the ILE!  Right now June may seem far off, but trust me, the time of your life is right around the corner!  I am so excited for all of you!  Now that Ryan has covered some helpful logistical tips (Which I recommend you read and follow.), I would like to tell you about some things that I took away from the ILE that continue to impact my life on a daily basis.
I like to think of the ILE as an unforgettable personal journey where each individual is tasked with discovering his or her passion for Ireland in a unique way.  When you return and hear mention of Ireland in others’ conversations, you’ll want to join in and exclaim your love of the country, describing every detail of the incredible journey you took on the ILE.  Now, speaking from experience, not everyone is as zealous about their heritage as others are, but immerse yourself in every opportunity and you will understand why daydreaming about Ireland is my favorite past time.
Now, most of you probably elected to apply for this program.  Just in case anyone feels they’ve been forced into applying (Just go with it.), or if you’re just still feeling nervous or hesitant about the experience (Totally normal.), let me put you at ease and dispel some myths you might believe about Ireland, study abroad trips, and new experiences in general.
Myth:  “I’m too shy to be myself around strangers,” or “Everyone will think I am weird if I open up and act myself.” 
Fact:  Everyone is in the same boat during the first few days, and alienating yourself from others is one of the most detrimental things you can do to your time on the ILE.  Keep an open mind, be friendly, open and engaged towards everyone, and most of all, be prepared to get to know others deeply.  Have a positive attitude from the very beginning of the program, and you will form fast (But lasting and incredible.) friendships.
Myth:  “I will have nothing in common with anyone.”
Fact:  There was a diverse range of people who were in my program, with kids from literally every corner of the United States, but we all shared a common Irish heritage and/or love of the country!  All it takes is one common thread to ignite the possibility to develop an amazing bond.  Again, just be open.
Myth:  “I’m not even going to attempt Irish dancing…, I have two left feet.”
Fact:  While you very well could have two left feet, no one really cares.  It might be good for some laughs during Irish Dance workshops!  Just give it your best shot.  Everyone likes different things, but there is something for everyone to connect with on the ILE.  No, your dancing skills may not belong in Riverdance, you might think literature is boring and dry, or your athletic prowess may be lacking…, I get it.  But make a promise to yourself to give every single activity your best effort and keep an open mind.  You may end up catching onto a jig, smirking at James Joyce’s humor, or helping your team towards a late night soccer game victory. (Oh-make sure you participate in the late night soccer games, even if you’ve never kicked a ball in your life.  SO fun and I’m no Sporty Spice, trust me.)  It’s a tired phrase, but it’s crazy true and I’ll end with it anyways:  You’ll never know until you try.  
Fiona Tomlin-San Diego, CA-ILE 2011
***More to come from Fiona tomorrow!***
