title: Helpful Advice from ILE 2011 Alumnus, Ryan Cueller!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hey 2012 ILE’ers!
Alright, so let’s begin with what I learned.  Basically anything about the country is fair game.  Considering you have six classes, you’ll basically cover everything there is to learn about Ireland.  It all starts with Irish literature in the morning.  We have to get the classes out of the way and you do a couple more.  Then you break for lunch and chill for an hour or two in between your morning and afternoon classes.  Once you’re back together, it’s back to some good ol’ Irish dancing and Gaelic sports.  
Besides the classes, literally everything you do should be cherished.  It didn’t hit me until I came back home of how much of a blast I had. At first, I thought this trip might be a tad bit lame, but in all reality I was completely wrong.  If there was one trip I could relive…, this would be that trip.  This Irish Life Experience has opened my eyes to my entire heritage, the Irish culture, and lifestyle of others.  I could continue rambling on about how profound this trip was, but I would become boring due to my horrific grammatical and conventional errors. 
Some things I wished I knew beforehand would have included the following:
-Pack light.  Do not bring a different set of clothes for each day, because you’ll end up wearing maybe four of them.  Maybe a couple more, but not really.
-Make sure you receive at least one care package, so you can have your classic munchies from back home in the US or wherever you’re from.
-Bring a rain poncho for the drizzly and crumby days.
-Buy postcards and stamps and send them out on the first week to all the peeps you want to contact, because by the time you get home they will just be arriving by then.
-Don’t forget to bring money!  Money is highly useful when it comes to buying souvenirs and food.  Personally I brought Euros over in the first place, but you can take money out from an ATM while over in Ireland.  Or you can just bring a wad of Euros  for your entire trip.  It’s really your preference. 
-Do not forget to pack a pair of shoes that you do not care to get wrecked-due to the amount of rain Ireland has in showers. 
-Also, bring a pair of casual shoes for everyday walking. 
-Lastly, make sure you take advantage of taking numerous pictures.  As a guy, I took maybe 1:8 the amount of pictures the girls took, but that’s because they’re girls.  Point is, take A LOT of pictures, because you’ll want to look back and remember how your trip to Ireland was and reminisce the past! 
So that concludes my excerpt of suggestions and comments about the Irish Life Experience and Ireland itself.  Trust me-you will have no regrets coming on this Program.  It has changed my life and continues to do so everyday I reflect upon it.  Enjoy your stay in Ireland. If you stay in Dublin at the Boarding School, King’s Hospital and there’s a summer camp with different groups of kids from Denmark France, Germany, Italy and Spain-tell the Spanish girls “Hola,” for me. 
-Ryan Cuellar-Chicago, IL-ILE 2011

title: Introducing Amy Dever-Your 2012 Female Counselor
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hi 2012 ILE’ers!  My name is Amy Dever and I can’t even begin to tell you how excited I am and how blessed I feel to be a part of this summer’s ILE Program!  I was born and raised in Spokane, Washington, where I lived until I graduated high school.  I went to Carroll College in Helena, Montana, where I studied Math for Secondary Education.  
The summer after my junior year at Carroll, I had the opportunity to go on a Diocesan Mission in Santo Tomas, Guatemala with several of my peers.  We were there for 11 days and immersed ourselves in their culture.  It was an amazing and life changing opportunity and made me want to see more of our incredible world. 
I have always loved working with kids, especially teenagers, and now I have the privilege of doing that as my profession.  Soon after graduating from Carroll, I heard of a high school math position opening in Polson, Montana.  I decided to apply for it-not even imagining that I would be offered the job and end up teaching here.  So far, it has been a wonderful first year of teaching.  I teach Geometry and Pre-Algebra and I was also a Co-Head Coach of the Cheerleading Squad.  
One of my most favorite hobbies is dancing and I will soon be getting my Zumba certification in June-only a few days before we take off on our great adventure to the Emerald Isle.  You know what that means…, there may be sporadic Zumba parties in Ireland!  I hope you’re ready for that!  
Although I have many roots in Ireland from both my mother’s and father’s sides of my family and many of my family members from the United States have been to Ireland, I have never traveled there.  I am so excited to embark on this journey and share this experience with all of you!  I can’t wait to meet you all very soon!

title: A Fun-Filled Reunion Weekend Had By All!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On March 9th, 60 Irish Life Experience and Irish Way Alumni gathered in Boston for a fun-filled Reunion Weekend.  A perfect kick-off to the St. Patrick’s Day Season-just around the corner. 
With many years being represented, from 1976-2011, Alumni traveled from as far away as Arizona, California, and Washington.  Special guest, Angela Mervyn-Coordinator and Teacher since 1998-even made the journey from Belfast, Northern Ireland.  A wonderful surprise to all that spent time and witnessed this remarkable woman in action on the program.  “Angie was an integral part in making my summer in Ireland so incredible.  It was amazing to see her after all these years,” said Caitlin Hawley (’03-San Francisco, CA).  Counselors Cyrus Anderson (’99, ’06, and ‘07-Alexis, IL), Orla Kennedy (’00 and ’06-Boston, MA), Kendall Drew (’03 and ’09-Chicago, IL), Siobhan Kennedy (’05 and ’10-Boston, MA), and Edel Coen (’11-San Francisco, CA) also made treasured appearances. 
The Reunion began with an All-Year Social at Anthem Kitchen and Bar in Faneuil Hall.  Alumni were reunited over a few pints, a slideshow of candids throughout the years, and a delicious dinner.  Heartfelt speeches were made and Alumni reminisced and shared stories of their magical summer spent on the Emerald Isle.  It was evident that the program had…, and continues to impact the Alumni in profound ways. 
It was early to bed, early to rise, as everyone was anxious to prepare for the 4th Annual Irish Pub Challenge on Saturday-sponsored by Tenon Tours-official travel partner of the program.  With an outstanding turnout of almost 4,000 people and 24 pubs participating; Boston’s Irish Pub Challenge came close to breaking the Guinness Book of World Records. 
Beginning at 10 AM at the Place, Alumni and Celebrity Captains from the Real World Challenges meandered their way through the streets of Beantown, checking into each pub, and enjoying a Guinness or two.  The goal was to visit as many pubs as possible for the chance to win a free trip to Ireland.  “I’m very impressed and proud to see how much the Irish Pub Challenge has grown.  I was also delighted to have Alumni representing the Irish Life Experience and Irish Way.  It is such a phenomenal program and we enjoyed having them participate in the event,” said Bryan Lewis, President of Tenon Tours.   
“It was a great weekend,” said Ryan Raines (’07-Rutherford, NJ).  “I can’t wait for the next Reunion,” said Maria Leal (’03-Boston, MA).  Kendall Drew (’03-Chicago, IL) said, “I cannot thank you enough for organizing such a fantastic weekend.  We all had such a great time!  It really reminded me of all the great memories, but also the impact that this program has had on my life, both as a student and a Counselor.”  “The Reunion was packed full of fun, laughs, and great energy that go hand in hand with the program.  And in typical Irish Life Experience/Irish Way style, I finished the weekend having made new friendships, while strengthening existing ones,” said Edel Coen (’11-San Francisco, CA). 
It was remarkable to see how many attended the Reunion and to hear how special the program is to each Alumni.  Angela Mervyn summed the program up well when she said it changes lives.  “It truly does.  It changes lives for the better. It changed mine and I will never forget this summer of a lifetime,” said Raizel Burstein-Frame (’11-Seattle, WA).
We are already planning the next Reunion.  Possibly in Ireland, so stay tuned.

title: The Pirate Princess
author: tharrison
content_raw:
In August 1593 a 63 year old Irish Queen and accused pirate sailed up the Thames River in England to demand a meeting with Queen Elizabeth to save her fortune and family.  Her name was Granuaile but the English called her Grace O’Malley.  The Virgin Queen met with the Pirate Queen and although not much is known about what they talked about, Granuaile emerged from the meeting with an order to release her family and leave her alone for the rest of her days. Grace O’Malley’s story has been mostly lost to history.
On the eve of her twelfth birthday Meg Murphy was woken up by the sound of a loud crash upon her house, which becomes the first in a string of otherworldly events that will blur the line of reality in her young life.  The very next day she receives a mysterious gift from her grandmother that will send her on an incredible journey to discover more about her family, the gift, and the famous 16th century Pirate Queen, Granuaile.
Proglogue
Boom!
A loud crack bounced off the walls.  She could almost feel the remnants of the sound from under her blanket, as she shot up straight in bed with indrawn breath. What in the world was that?  A quick look around her room revealed that nothing had fallen off her shelves or from the top of her dresser.  Frightened, she looked around again, nothing was out of place but…, Finn!  The indentation on her comforter at the foot of her bed was empty.  Her heart was pounding from the noise that woke her and the realization that her dog was not where he should be, made it worse.  Where did that dog go?  The door was closed and so was the closet, so he had to be in the room somewhere.  She got up from her bed and walked towards the silver light that was coming from the alcove where her window was, and sure enough, there was her big white dog. He was up on his hind legs leaning on the windowsill. His ears were perked up and he was looking out the window, as if he were searching for what made that terrible crash that woke them both.
It was a bang or knock or something, and whatever it was, it was really loud.  A tree must have fallen on the house.  She stood next to Finn and looked out on the beautiful scenery that was the view from her room.  The moon was shining its light on the water beyond the back yard and a gentle breeze was leading the trees in a slow dance back and forth.  The peaceful scene helped to calm her nerves from the scare but going back to bed was not an option at this point because she was wide awake.  She had to find what woke her.
“Come on boy.” She said to her dog and they headed towards the closed bedroom door. The warm brass knob in her hand turned without a squeak, and Meg peeked her head out of the doorway.
Nothing.  No lights were on and no one was out in the hall.  Someone else had to have heard it.  She grabbed Finn’s collar and lead him to her little brother’s room that was right next to her’s.  The old hinges let out a creak as she pushed the door open, but even that noise didn’t wake up the little boy sleeping peacefully in his crib.  Are you kidding me?  It didn’t even wake the baby!  She went further down the hall and it was the same situation with her parents and her big sister also.  All were sleeping undisturbed in their beds, oblivious to the natural disaster that must have struck the old Victorian house.
Was it a dream?
No way!
It could not have been a dream because Finn heard it too.  A branch or a limb from one of the tall trees that surrounded them had to have fallen on the roof, and her family was going to be very surprised to find out that they had slept through such a racket.  This could not wait until morning.  She had to find out what had made the noise.
Meg quietly made her way down the staircase to the first floor.  The house was silent but the loud knock still echoed in her head.  She looked out of the window next to the front door and found nothing out of the ordinary, again.  As they tiptoed down the hall towards the kitchen, the tick tacking of Finn’s paws on the hardwood floors was the only sound in the house.  They walked through the kitchen, where nothing was disturbed either, and Meg decided that they better go outside to take a look at the house from afar, to survey the damage.  She slid the heavy glass patio door open with a rumble and walked out into the cool autumn night with her dog close behind. 
The wind blew her hair around as she stepped onto the stone patio.  The peaceful sound of chirping crickets and waves lapping the shore greeted her.  The serenity was broken only by the ringing of navigational bells rolling over the water from a buoy in the distance.  Meg had never been outside of her house alone at night, and her senses were extremely alert.  The breeze that moved the trees and her hair carried with it the smell of the salt water and the decaying fall leaves that were everywhere.  It was a strange earthy ocean mix.  She walked across the patio towards the backyard, which slanted down to the water’s edge.
There was a silver streak of reflected moonlight that ran across the water from their shore, across the sound, to the island in the distance where her grandmother lived.  It was like a magical bridge suspended on the waves that she could walk on to go and visit her Nanny.  Meg shook her head to get back to reality; she was out here for a reason.
Finn and she walked just far enough away to get a better look at the whole house behind them.  She turned around and was disappointed to see the roof of her home was completely undamaged.  No branches or limbs were lying across the old house anywhere.
But the crash had happened!
A stiff gust blew in from the water with a whoosh startling her.  Meg felt a sort of tension in the air which made her uncomfortable. Even Finn was uneasy.  He was standing tight against her leg with his ears perked up and he let out a soft whimper.  There had to be something on the other side of the house.  Although she was starting to get a little scared again her curiosity got the best of her and she pressed on.
They walked through the grass and leaves, alert to anything strange, and looked up at the old house with its many gables.  The stars that shone brightly above, along with the moon, illuminated everything they looked at with a surreal blue grey tint. There was magic to the fall night around them.  The temperature was cool, but not enough for Meg to be cold, and all of the sounds and smells added to the mystery that surrounded her walk.  She expected to find the source of the crash at every turn of a corner but by the time they got back around to the patio in the back yard finding nothing, she decided to give up the search.  Maybe it was her imagination?
Her father was standing at the door to the kitchen as she slid the patio door closed.  “What are you doing honey?”  He looked at her over crossed arms.  “It’s the middle of the night and you should not be going outside by yourself.”
“Daaad,” Meg replied in the sing songy way only a little girl can address her father “I was checking out the loud crash that woke us up and I am almost twelve and can go outside by myself!”
“Even tomorrow, when you turn twelve, you are not allowed to go outside by yourself at night and the only sound that woke me up, was the sound of the sliding glass door to the patio opening.”  He looked at her under forced furrowed brows and a smirk that showed he was not really mad at her.
“You didn’t hear that earth shattering knock, like something hit our house?”
“No sweetie,” said her father. He reached into the refrigerator and poured a glass of milk which he handed to her, “It must have been a dream.  It’s time to go back to bed, we have a big day ahead of us tomorrow.”
“But Dad, even Finn heard it,” she said gulping down the milk and placing the cup in the sink.  Her father looked down at the dog.  Finn wagged its tail at him and he scratched his head.
“Maybe you knocked one of the dolls off your bed and onto the floor?”
“I don’t sleep with dolls anymore Daddy!” 
He swept her up in his arms and started back upstairs. “I can’t believe my little baby doesn’t sleep with her dolls anymore.  It seems like just yesterday there was a virtual stuffed army at the foot of your bed standing guard over you.  Now my big twelve year old is all grown up and doesn’t need them anymore.”
“I have Finn now Daddy and will always have you guarding me!”
That put a big smile on her dad’s face.  He walked Meg into her room then lowered her into bed.  She pulled up the sheets and her dad gave her a kiss. “Sweet dreams” he said while walking out, shutting the door behind him.
“It had to be something, huh Finn?” she said to her dog as he snuggled into the foot of her bed.  The dog looked up at her with his big dark eyes in agreement and after some tossing and turning they eventually fell back to sleep.

title: Aran-tastic!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
One of the highlights of the Irish Life Experience is a trip to the Aran Islands.  The Aran Islands are a group of three islands located at the mouth of Galway Bay.  From west to east they are: Inishmore, Inishmaan, and Inisheer and Irish is the main spoken language on all three islands.
On Monday, we set sail from Rossaveal for a fun filled day of biking around the island of Inishmore-the largest of the three islands.  We arrived around 10:30 AM and rented bikes for all of the students.  From there, everyone was able to enjoy their packed lunches and explore the island on their own-all by nine miles in length and two miles in width.  It rained for the first hour we were on the island, but once again the skies opened up and the sun once shone down upon the Irish Life Experience.  
The islands’ geology is mainly karst limestone and is thus closely related to the Burren.  Huge boulders up to 80 feet above the sea at parts of the west facing cliffs have been shown not to be glacial erratics as originally believed, but rather as an extreme form of storm beach, cast there by giant waves that occur on average once per century.
A lacework of ancient stone walls enfolds all three islands to contain local livestock.  Also found are early clocháns-dry-stone beehive huts from the early-Christian period.  Enda of Aran founded the first true Irish Monastery near Killeany.  In time there were a dozen monasteries on Inishmore alone.  Many Irish saints had some connection with Aran.  St. Brendan was blessed for his voyage there, Jarlath of Tuam, Finnian of Clonard, and St. Columba called it the “Sun of the West.”
Since the islands were first populated in larger numbers, probably at the time of the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland in the mid 17th century, when the Catholic population of Ireland had the choice of going “to hell or to Connaght,” many fled to the numerous islands off the west coast of Ireland.  There they adapted themselves to the raw climatic conditions, developing a survival system of total self-sufficiency.  Their methods included mixing layers of sand and seaweed on top of rocks to create fertile soil, a technique used to grow potatoes and other vegetables.  The same seaweed method also provided grazing grass within stone-wall enclosures for cattle and sheep, which in turn provided wool and yarn to make handwoven trousers, skirts and jackets, hand-knitted sweaters, shawls, caps, and hide shoes.  The islanders also constructed unique boats for fishing, building their thatched cottages from the materials available or trading with the mainland.
Many Irish Life Experience students went to Dún Aonghasa.  Dún Aonghasa is the most famous of several prehistoric forts on the Aran Islands.  It is located on the top of a 250 foot cliff and is an important archaeological site that also offers a spectacular view. It is not known when Dún Aonghasa was built, though it is now thought to date from the Iron Age.  It was probably originally constructed as a circular ringfort several hundred feet from the coast, its present precarious position being the result of centuries of coastal erosion.
The fort consists of a series of four concentric walls of dry stone construction.  Surviving stonework is twelve feet wide at some points.  The original shape was presumably oval or D-shaped but parts of the cliff and fort have since collapsed into the sea.  Outside the third ring of walls lie a defensive system of stone slabs, known as a ‘Chevaux de frise,’ planted in an upright position in the ground and still largely well-preserved.  These ruins also feature a huge rectangular stone slab, the function of which is unknown.  Impressively large among prehistoric ruins, the outermost wall of Dún Aonghasa encloses an area of approximately 14 acres.  Although clearly defensible, the particular location of Dún Aonghasa suggests that its primary purpose was religious and ceremonial rather than military.  It may have been used for seasonal rites by the druids, perhaps involving the bonfires that could be seen from the mainland of Ireland.
Students soaked up the gorgeous views and cautiously laid close to the edge of the cliffs, inhaling the fresh Irish sea air.  Joe said it was more impressive and untouched than the Cliffs of Moher and Sydney said it was one of her favorite days of the whole program.  
On the three mile journey back to the village of Inishmore, students stopped at a beautiful beach to go swimming and collect shells, looked through a telescope at the seal colony vantage point, took pictures of donkeys and horses, picked flowers, and fixed chains on their bikes.  Eventually, everyone returned to the port, where they enjoyed banana and Nutella crepes as a treat.  Rough waters provided a fun trip back to the mainland, but students were able to get a bird’s eye view from sitting on top of the Aran ferry.  We arrived back to Gort na Coiribe, exhausted after an incredible experience and a few rosy cheeks.  It was simply a spectacular day!

title: Dan Parkinson: A life, turmoil, and redemption
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Life is full of choices, albeit, many of those choices are frequently wrong, illegal, or an affront to the laws of man, but Dan has been a man that makes choices and those choices frequently find themselves on the far side of the rainbow, as the tattoos on his lower back suggests.  After years as an advocate for many causes, among them his unflagging support for the dental rights on gypsies, the continual utility of ravens, and of course his most infamous support for the utilization of pedophiles in bell choirs, for which we are thankful.
     Nevertheless, these choices have been difficult.  Dan’s shining back is the result of thousands of pumus stones, for which he received the derision of many of his peers, but in the educational community Dan’s decisions have been received with many a hearty pat on the back or that peculiar high five he has received in the men’s room along the beautiful shores of Youghal.
     As a founding and integral member of the irish life experience, Dan has found that the legal peculiarities of european law have afforded him the wonderful opportunity to work with and educate, no matter how violently, the creme de la creme of the America’s future dancers and poets. Dan’s nearly twenty-four hour support and vigilance has resulted in a new wave of emotionally scarred and intellectually feeble generation of clerks and tug-jobbers.  Dan is most fulfilled when he knows that his perseverence, close attention, and vigorous hand on thigh contact has influenced a generation of internet experts and Irish academics.

title: Hello from Galway!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
The Irish Life Experience left for Galway on Saturday morning-bright and early. The wonderful, Brian Farrell from Burren Coaches, picked us up and we were delighted to see him. He is a treasured friend of the ILE and is absolutely wonderful. He does a fantastic job guiding the students around the west of Ireland.
We arrived into Galway in the afternoon-while listening to Steve Earle’s Galway Girl to set the mood-and gave the students their food stipend for the next few days. After they got the apartments situated at Gort na Coiribe and were settled, they had free time to wander across the road to Dunne’s-where they would do their grocery shopping for the week. When they returned, many of them made delicious meals for each other. Spaghetti and meatballs, grilled cheese, and scones-were just some of the items on the menu that evening. Zoe made a delicious Italian feast, while Jenny said she can’t wait to whip up a lemon chicken and angel hair pasta dish. Taryn knows what apartment she will be visiting in the next few days;).
After the long travel day, students were in bed early before their first tour during the Galway portion. We left for Connemara on Sunday for a few wee hours and left with many memories to treasure. Our first stop was a brief photo opportunity at Kylemore Abbey. Kylemore is a Benedictine monastery founded in 1920 on the grounds of Kylemore Castle. The Abbey was founded for Benedictine Nuns who fled Belgium in World War I.
Prior to Kylemore becoming an Abbey, it was built as a Castle and private home for the family of Mitchell Henry, a wealthy politician from Manchester, England who was also MP for Galway County from 1871 to 1885.
The Castle covered approximately 40,000 square feet with over 70 rooms and the principal wall was two to three feet thick. The facade measured 142 feet in length and is made of granite brought from Dalkey by sea to Letterfrack and limestone from Ballinasloe. There were 33 bedrooms, 4 bathrooms, 4 sitting rooms, ballroom, billard room, library, study, school room, smoking room, gun room and various offices and domestic staff residences for the butler, cook, housekeeper and other servants.
In 1920, Kylemore became an Abbey and is the oldest of the Irish Benedictine Abbeys. The community of nuns, who have resided here for 189 years, have a long history stretching back almost three hundred and forty years. Founded in Ypres, Belgium, in 1665, the purpose of the Abbey at Ypres was to provide an education and religious community for Irish women during times of persecution here in Ireland. Down through the centuries, Ypres Abbey attracted the daughters of the Irish nobility, both as students and postulants, and enjoyed the patronage of many influential Irish families living in exile.
Here the nuns opened an international boarding school and established a day school for local girls, which closed in June 2010. Since the 70’s, the Benedictine Community have opened their Abbey and Estate to the public and now Kylemore has become known as a must see when visiting the West of Ireland.
Next was a lunch break in the quaint town of Clifden. Students enjoyed meandering through the streets and MC and Zoe did an impromptu modeling shoot with their matching pink wellies. Epic!
The final stop was Dan O’Hara Heritage Center. Built on the site of the original cottage home of Dan from Connemara-renowned in the popular Irish ballad all over the world.
Along with his wife and seven children, Dan lived in this tiny cottage and the family were self-sufficient even in times when poverty stalked most other areas of Ireland in the early 1840’s.
On the eight acre farm the O’Hara family had their own crops, they had the usual array of farm animals as well as ducks and hens around the farmyard.
The turf for the fire was also cut in the local bog by Dan, and in the flickering firelight of Dan O’Hara’s kitchen many a marriage stemmed from relationships developing into romance at the Ceili dances in this Connemara kitchen which was the the Ballroom of Romance of another era.
But the tranquillity was suddenly shattered by the dreaded “battering ram” and the landlord who laid his old home low when Dan was unable to pay the exorbitant rent demanded by his superiors after it was discovered he had modernized his little home in 1845.
Dan, his wife and seven young children had to abandon their homeland and work for their passage on an emigrant ship bound for New York. Sadly his wife and three of their children died on that terrible journey.
With his four children fostered out to American families, Dan was a broken man selling matches on the streets of New York-a far cry from the tranquillity that his family had enjoyed in scenic Connemara.
Now the cottage has been restored to it’s past glory. Irish Life Experience students were invited to step back into the past in this traditional Dan O’Hara cottage and the music, merriment and memories of another era came floating back in their mind’s eye.
Martin, our wonderful host, took the students on a tractor ride to soak in the gorgeous views of Connemara, showed them how to cut turf, told them about Dan O’Hara, sang a few wee songs, and challenged them to a tug-a-war. Angie’s team ended up winning. Only by default, since she convinced them to drop the rope after a few minutes into the war. Students even had a horseshoe throwing contest, and Molly won the grand prize of delicious Irish chocolates for getting TWO horseshoes around a stake.
It was a great day for the ILE!

title: Protected: Northern Ireland Bliss
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Thursday, the students went north to Belfast, the Giant’s Causeway, and Carrick-a-rede Rope Bridge.  Angie served as our incredible tour guide when we passed through her hometown of Belfast.  She pointed out the Shankhill and Falls Road and wow’ed us with tons of information.  She also showed the students the ship yards where the Titanic was built and mentioned that next year marks the 100th Anniversary of the Titanic.
Continuing to make our way further north, the ILE Staff played a competitive game of dog and tractor.  One point for spotting a dog, one point for spotting a tractor, and if you spot a dog in a tractor; you win the game.  As you can see, we are easily entertained.  
The drive from Belfast up to the Giant’s Causeway was very scenic-passing by little farms just clinging to the tops of cliffs overlooking the sea.  Beyond Rathlin Island in the hazy distance-the coastline of Scotland was just visible.  MC was thrilled to see another country so close, even though it was shrouded in the mist.  Upon arriving at the Giant’s Causeway, the students grabbed a quick lunch in order to build up their strength for the walk.  The walk to the Causeway is steep and hilly, but it is well worth it.  
The Giant’s Causeway is an area of roughly 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, the result of an ancient volcanic eruption.  In a 2005 poll of Radio Times readers, the Giant’s Causeway was named as the fourth greatest natural wonder in the United Kingdom.  The tops of the columns form stepping stones that lead from the cliff foot and disappear under the sea. Most of the columns are hexagonal, although there are also some with four, five, seven and eight sides.  The tallest are about 36 feet high, and the solidified lava in the cliffs is 70 feet thick in places.  
Some 50 to 60 million years ago, during the Paleogene period, Antrim was subject to intense volcanic activity, when highly fluid molten basalt intruded through chalk beds to form an extensive lava plateau.  As the lava cooled rapidly, contraction occurred.  While contraction in the vertical direction reduced the flow thickness, horizontal contraction could only be accommodated by cracking throughout the flow.  The size of the columns is primarily determined by the speed at which lava from a volcanic eruption cools. The extensive fracture network produced the distinctive columns seen today.  The basalts were originally part of a great volcanic plateau called the Thulean Plateau which formed during the Paleogene period.
While many people believe the geological interpretation of how the Giant’s Causeway was formed, Angie prefers the legend instead.  It is said that Irish warrior Fionn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool) built the Causeway to walk to Scotland to fight his Scottish counterpart Benandonner.  After seeing Benandonner’s great bulk, Fionn asked his wife to disguise him as the baby.  When Benandonner saw the size of the ‘infant’, he assumed the alleged father, Fionn, must be gigantic indeed.  Therefore, Benandonner fled home in terror, ripping up the Causeway in case he was followed by Fionn.  See…, isn’t the legend much more entertaining?
The ILE soaked in all of the gorgeous views at the Giant’s Causeway and many said it was their favorite place thus far.  We took many pictures by the Organ, Giant’s Boot, Giant’s Eyes, and the Shepherd’s Steps.  
Fiona said that is was a very majestic sight.  The sun peeked through the clouds, so it was easy to lay back and marvel at the strange formations of stone.  Once they climbed back up to the car park, they boarded the bus and headed a short way down the road to Carrick-a-Rede Rope Bridge.  
Carrick-a-Rede Rope Bridge is a rope suspension bridge near Ballintoy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland.  The bridge links the mainland to the tiny Carrick Island.  The site is owned and maintained by the National Trust, spans sixty-five feet and is ninety-eight feet above the rocks below.  Today the bridge is mainly a tourist attraction, with 247,000 visitors in 2009.  
Carrick-a-rede means “rock in the road.”  It is thought salmon fishermen have been erecting bridges to the island for over 350 years. It has taken many forms.  In the 1970’s it featured only a single handrail and large gaps between the slats.  A version of the bridge, tested up to ten tonnes, was built with the help of local climbers and abseilers in 2000.  A subsequent design was engineered in 2004 and offers visitors and fishermen alike a much safer passage to the island. The current wire rope and Douglas fir bridge was made by Heyn Construction in Belfast and erected early in 2008 at a cost of over £16,000.  Although no one has fallen off the bridge, there have been many instances where visitors, unable to face the walk back across the bridge, have had to be taken off the island by boat.
Crossing the bridge is not for the faint of heart and there were definitely a few weak knees at the thought.  Alyssa said she was proud to make it over the bridge with dry pants.  Fi screamed the entire way across, but she made it!  The area is exceptional in natural beauty with stunning views.  
We finished our tour for the day with a stop at Ballycastle, just as it started to downpour.  The students each received a dinner stipend.  Fish and chips seemed to be the popular choice on the menu for most of the ILE’ers, followed by a quick stop at the candy shop.
After dinner, we decided it was time to head back to Dublin, before it got too late.  During the next few hours, Angie serenaded us with a few tunes from ACDC and Mama Mia.  We are just trying to groom the students for the many sing songs we will be having on the west coast during our Holidays.  We finally returned back to King’s Hospital in Dublin at 10:00 PM.  I don’t know how they did it-I was exhausted-but the students decided they had enough energy to go dance at the King’s Hospital Disco.  Amazing!
What a magnificent day!

title: Protected: Choc-a-bloc with Workshops!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Wednesday was our final class day of the trip.  After this, it’s all holidays!  But we had work to do and prizes to win before the real fun could begin.  Angie started the morning out with her Northern Ireland Workshop.  The students were greatly impressed by her use of the interactive whiteboard as she gave her run through of the “Troubles” up North.  The students would find this information invaluable on Thursday for their trip up to the Giant’s Causeway and Carrick-a-rede Rope Bridge.  Sallie said that Angie explained the “Troubles” from both sides and that it was very interesting.  A few said that they never really heard much about what had happened in Northern Ireland, so this helped them gain a better perspective-from someone who grew up in Belfast during this time.  
For the final Irish class, Dan organized a very complicated came called Bingo in Gaelic.  They first learned the numbers 1-10 in Gaelic-a haon, a dó, a trí, a ceathair, a cúig, a sé, a seacht, a hocht, a naoi, a deich.  After a tense battle and despite Sallie’s accusations of a conspiracy, Kelly won the competition and with it a collection of Oscar Wilde’s plays.  Congrats Kel!
In Taryn’s Irish Studies class, the students gave speeches about anything that had surprised them since they came to Ireland.  Evo’s imitation of Angie’s Belfast accent got some laughs and Fiona’s dissertation on Irish style (or lack thereof:) proved a great hit.   Kelly gave instructions on how to make the perfect cup or cuppa tea, while MC demonstrated how to draw the perfect leprechaun.  It was a lot of fun and the students really enjoyed it!
The presentations continued in Dan’s Irish American History class.  Tom gave a great presentation and on Gene Tunney and Evan surprised nobody by chossing John McEnroe as his Irish-American hero. Ultimately, Jenny won the prize-a collection of Yeats’ poems-for her eloquent speech on Annie Sullivan, Helen Keller’s tutor. 
The rest of the day was choc-a-bloc with workshops.  Taryn gave two seperate workshops on Celtic Crafts where Olivia painted a lovely picture frame.  Royal blue for the national color of Ireland, with the ILE logo, and all of the 2011 students names painted on it.  MC also painted the Irish flag with ILE 2011.  The creativity continued with the painting of pots.  Kelsey painted a gorgeous pot that she is looking forward to planting shamrocks in when she returns home.  
Shortly after, the group was honored by the presence of former ILE teacher and champion Irish tin whistle player and dancer, Corinna O’Donoghue. Corinna misses the program so much, that every year she comes back for more.  
Dunners, Prunes, Sasha Fierce, and Zoe-inator took Corinna’s amazing Tin Whistle Workshop.  The girls learned how to play a scale, Óró Sé do Bheatha ‘Bhaile, and the Kerry Polka on a Tin Whistle in D.  Sasha picked it up very quickly with her musical background, while Kelsey loved it and said she can’t wait to learn some more songs.  
Our two ILE dancers, Kel and Prunes, were particularly keen to try out the moves they  had seen last night at Riverdance.  Corinna taught them a very fast reel and they both enjoyed the Advanced Irish Dancing Workshop.  We are looking forward to them showing off their new moves after they practice a few more times.  
After dinner had digested, Dan ran his world famous Rugby Workshop.  There was great disappointment from the boys and Jenny when he informed everyone that it would be a non-contact version they would be playing.  Dan went over the rules and techniques, then they practiced with some warm-up exercises, before having a short scrimmage against each other.  Sallie and Tom, once again proved to me the athletic champs for their team, while he said that Kelsey and Prunes had the most heart and showed the most improvement.  At the end, Dan showed the students how to form a scrum in rugby, which most thought was hilarious.  Despite the physical exertions of the rugby, students still had enough energy for a talent show.  More to come on that in the next post.

title: Protected: My Heart is Dublin for Ireland!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
The Irish Life Experience spent Tuesday in Dublin.  Students had the option of doing various tours throughout the day, such as the Book of Kells, Dublin Castle, Jameson Distillery, the Guinness Brewery, the National Art Museum, and St. Patrick’s Cathedral.  Many spent their time wisely, exploring the historical sites of Dublin first, before shopping for Irish souvenirs.  
Half of them began with a tour of the Guinness Brewery.  This is one of the most popular visits in town and is a beer lover’s Disneyland-a multimedia bells-and-whistles homage to the country’s most famous export and the city’s most enduring symbol.  The massive 26-hectare St. Jame’s Gate Brewery is a suitable cathedral in which to worship the black gold; shaped like a giant pint of Guinness.  It rises seven impressive stories high around a stunning central atrium.  At the top is the head-represented by the Gravity Bar-with a panoramic view of Dublin.  
Students were able to walk through the extravaganza-involving an array of audiovisual and interactive displays that cover pretty much all aspects of the brewery’s history and the process.  
We decided to let the three 18 year olds-Alyssa, Molly, and Sallie-“Pour the Perfect Pint” when they reached the top.  They received a certificate of approval and were even able to have a small taste of Guinness at the end.  Just a wee sip.
After shopping for Guinness souvenirs, it was off to the city center.  Jenny, Kelly, and Kelsey decided to visit the Book of Kells as Trinity’s top show-stopper.  The Book of Kells is an illuminated manuscript, dating from AD 800 and therefore one of the oldest books in the world.  It was probably produced by monks at St. Colmcille’s Monastery on the remote island of Iona-off the western coast of Scotland.  Repeated looting by marauding Vikings forced the monks to flee to the temporary safety of Kells, County Meath, in AD 806, along with their masterpiece.  
The Book of Kells contains the four Gospels of the New Testament, as well as prefaces, summaries, and other text.  The extensive and amazingly complex illustrations make it unique.  The superbly decorated opening initials are only part of the story-for the book has smaller illustrations between the lines.  “Even though there were only two pages shown, it was so impressive,” Kelsey said! 
Before we knew it, it was time to go back to King’s Hospital.  Everyone seemed to really enjoy their time in the city and many want to return very soon.  Tom said that the architecture in Dublin was deadly.  Olivia agreed and said she thought the buildings were ornate and loved the history.  “I simply just loved the overall vibe Bro,” Ryan said.  “I loved all of the trendy styles,” said Skoot.  Sallie said that her favorite shop was Knobs and Knockers.  Molly Fitz also added that Monsoon and Top Shop were fantastic for good sales on fashionable clothes.  Alyssa, ODawg, and Zoe told us they went to Bewely’s and had an incredible lunch.  Fiona discovered Lemon and exclaimed they had the best crepes-simply deelish!  Connor let us know that he went to Burger King and got a cool crown that he wore for the rest of the day.  What a silly guy!  We love you Con Man.  Evo said that Dublin might be his new favorite city in fact.  What a great day we had in Ireland’s capital.   
In fact, the day was so good-that many students decided to go to Riverdance at the Gaiety later that evening.  Riverdance is a famous theatrical show consisting of traditional Irish stepdancing, notable for its rapid leg movements while body and arms are kept largely stationary.  It originated as an interval performance during the 1994 Eurovision Song Contest, a moment that is still considered a significant watershed in Irish culture.  Riverdance is, in essence, the story of the Irish culture and of the Irish immigration to America.  For Irish dancers, Kelly and Raizel, Riverdance was extremely special.  Not to mention to see it in Ireland.  Kelly said that she was moved to tears by the performance, while Raizel said it was magical.

title: Protected: Croker and Howth!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Monday, students were able to get a tour of Croke Park.  Croke Park is a magnificent stadium-if your impressed by them is Ireland’s largest and fourth largest in Europe.  Seating 82,000, Croker-as it’s lovingly known in Dublin-is the fabulous fortress that protects the sanctity and spirit of Gaelic games in Ireland, as well as the administrative HQ of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA).  The students learned that the GAA considers itself not just the governing body of a bunch of Irish games, but also the stout defender of a cultural identity that is ingrained in Ireland’s sense of self.  
Alyssa said it was especially interesting exploring the inside walls of the stadium after watching the Leinster Finals there the day before.  Kelly said she enjoyed the locker room and seeing all of the jerseys from the different counties.  The students were fascinated to learn that there are actually 34 counties in the GAA.  Some of them were confused, since they know that there are only 32 counties in Ireland.  Brendan, our fantastic tour guide, cleared up any confusion and told us that London and New York City are also included in the GAA.  Kelsey said that she was impressed by the Waterford Crystal chandelier in the Player’s Lounge.  The chandelier had 34 Gaelic footballs-representing each of the 34 counties and 70 slithers-which signifies the 70 minutes in a hurling game-hanging from the ceiling.  There were also colors of red, orange, yellow, green, and blue-showing all of the different colors in flags and jerseys for each of the counties.  
After the tour, the group went to Howth for a hike.  Howth is a pretty fishing village and a popular excursion from Dublin.  The views from the top are magnificent.  
We started the hike at the summit and walked around the Ben of Howth-a headland near the village.  Jenny said there were incredible views across Dublin Bay-right down to County Wicklow-and wished she had more time to explore.   Taryn said we lucked out with the weather and managed to finish the hike right before it started lashing rain.  Perfect timing.  
The day concluded with a Quiz Night, which involved the Alpha and Stagewise groups at King’s Hospital.  The “ILE Babes” had some great rounds and Prunes and Sasha Fierce were able to get a lot of points in the Theatre category.  Even though they didn’t win, Ryan said that he enjoyed getting to know the other students in different groups.

title: Protected: Up the Dubs!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Sunday, students were able to relax and sleep in.  Yeah!  Evan said it was delightful to catch up on some much needed shut eye.  In the afternoon, the Irish Life Experience students were lucky enough to go to the Leinster Gaelic Football Finals at Croke Park-Dublin vs. Wexford.  It was a special treat and many said it was the best day yet.  Since Dan and Edel are from Dublin, they convinced the students to cheer for the Dubs.  The students dressed up in colors of blue and white and even painted their faces.  A few of them also bought matching blue leggings for 4 Euros at Penney’s and were ready to cheer on the Dubs in style.  Students stopped to buy Dublin flags and scarves on their way into the stadium from local vendors-to add to their attire.  The ILE were definitely proud supporters of Dublin-no doubt about it.  
Sasha Fierce said it was an incredible atmosphere at Croker.  Before the game began, the Irish National Anthem was sung.  Edel said it was such a special moment to see all of the Irish Life Experience students singing it by heart in Gaelic.  She was so honored to be a part of the program and a tad misty eyed.  “It’s amazing to see so many young Irish Americans interested in Irish culture and helping keep it alive,” she said.  
As the game went on, Ryan said it was fun to listen to the chants from both Dublin and Wexford.  Levi said he enjoyed belting out, “Come on ye boys in blue, come on ye boys in blue!”  “I’m going to marry a Gaelic football player.  They are studly,” Fiona chimed in.  Sallie agreed.  
It was a close game throughout, but in the end the Dubs pulled away and won the game with a score of 2-13 to 1-13.  Tom said he can’t wait for the All Ireland Finals and speculates that Dublin will be prime contenders for the trophy.  Raizel said it was an amazing day and summed it up by simply saying, “Up the Dubs!”
We ended the day by returning to King’s Hospital and having a brilliant game of Capture the Flag.  Levi said it was very exciting and he said both teams ended up winning one game each.  He gave mad props to Skoot for guarding his team’s flag!

title: Protected: Classes, Trad Music, and Discotheques=Deadly!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Saturday, Angie discussed WB Yeats and Seamus Heaney in her Irish literature class.  MC said that Angie is very knowledgeable and simply loves listening to her.  Raizel said it’s her favorite class.  
In Dan’s Gaelic class, students practiced the Irish National Anthem.  Students had to sing in pairs in front of the class and he was blown away by the gorgeous voices of Molly, Raizel, and Sasha.  They are very talented singers!
In Irish history class, Dan spoke about the Famine to the 1916 Rebellion.  Evan said he really enjoys Dan’s Irish history class, because he’s fascinated by Ireland’s past.
It was then time for Taryn’s Irish studies.  Taryn spoke about how Ireland has evolved over the past 20+ years and many students agreed that the Irish and Irish Americans are losing their identity in the modern world.  The students discussed what people associate Ireland and the Irish with-not necessarily good things.  They then shared what they want to teach their families and friends about Ireland and the Irish people-the culture, history, literature, and traditions…  Their final task was to make a promise to themselves when they return to the states on how they were going to improve Irish culture and keep it alive in their communities.  
Irish American history followed and the students talked about famous Irish Americans with Dan.  Catherine said she enjoys this class and learning about her ancestors.
In the afternoon, students were able to have free time at the Liffey Valley Shopping Center.  Many picked up blue leggings, shirts, and shorts.  Some even purchased Dublin jerseys.  You can tell what team everyone will be cheering for at the Leinster Finals.  Both Dan and Edel are from Dublin and told the students they would not be happy if they cheered for Wexford.  Up the Dubs!
Later that evening, Angie’s brother, Tom-came to visit us with his traditional Irish band from Belfast.  We were treated with magnificent tunes of jigs, hornpipes, and reels.  Music from banjos, buzukis, bodhrans, guitars, whistles and uilleann pipes echoed throughout the halls of King’s Hospital.  There was plenty of toe-tapping and it was music to our ears.  Tom, Paddy, Paul and Ryan introduced the students to each of the various unfamiliar instruments, before playing music that the students could practice their 3’s and 7’s they had learned in dance class.  Our Irish dancer, Kelly, performed a routine at the end of the sessiun.  Molly, Raizel, and Sasha even got up to sing traditional Irish songs in front of the group.  It was so special!  As much as the students didn’t want the music to end, Tom and his band bid adieu.  “Tom’s band was so amazing and I was honored to sing with the them,” said Raizel/Prunes.  Sallie said that the uilleann pipes are the shiz!
Students were then treated to their first discotheque at King’s Hospital.  Everyone got dressed up and got ready to show off their stellar dance skills.  It was a blast and the students loved the experience.  They can’t wait for more discos!

title: Protected: Letter Home
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Dan was very impressed with Sasha Fierce’s letter that she wrote in Irish American history and wanted to share.  Enjoy!  
August 1950
Ma,
I’ve entered into a world of grey.  Buildings, suits, complexions.  The weak tea I drink now every morning is no substitute for the hearth and fire of home.  I’ve landed a job in New York City at a tiny butcher’s shop tucked away in a side street-away from the roaring madness of the city.  My pay is minimal, but steady.  Enclosed is half of my earnings for the past year.  Hopefully, they will last longer than last year’s.  I’d hate to come home to an abandoned farm.
While Ireland wallows in depression, America seems to have climbed to the top of the economic world.  They talk of their own depression, as if they had born the brunt of all the suffering in the world.  They will never understand the pain of a truly suffering country.  Ireland is full of holes, whether they be in our pockets or our bodies.  Hopefully, they’ll all have healed sufficiently in five years time, when I make my journey back to the land of saints and scholars.  
Your Loving Daughter
(Sasha Kudler, CA)

title: Protected: Loving Dublin Life
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Friday was filled with classes in the morning.  In Dan’s Gaelic class, students learned the Irish for left=clé, right=deis, red=dearg, blue=gorm, yellow=buí, and green=glas-all in preparation for Twister.  It was savage-to quote the words of Edel.  Deadly, said Fiona.
In Irish history, students learned more from the 1798 Rebellion up to the Famine.  
Reeling in the Years is a fantastic DVD that Taryn showed in her class to give the students a perspective of what Ireland was like in the early 1990’s.  It showed highlights that were significant in Ireland a few years before most of our ILE’ers were even born.  Taryn will tie this DVD in with her class on Saturday to how Ireland has evolved over the past 20+ years.  
Irish American history was spent imagining what it would be like to emigrate to America during the Famine.  Students pretended to be emigrants and write letters back to their families in Ireland.  Dan said that Sasha Fierce wrote a brilliant and heartfelt letter.  Raizel/Prunes said she enjoyed this activity in class a lot.
During the afternoon, Dan and Edel taught the students how to play Gaelic football.  They went over the rules and scoring procedures, then practiced the basic skills of kicking and passing the ball.  All of the students picked up the sport very quickly.  It was then time for a quick scrimmage.  Molly expressed that she really isn’t much of a “sporty” person, but she really enjoyed the workshop.  She said she can’t wait for the football match at Croke Park.  Zoe said that it will be great to know all of the rules, before Sunday as well.  Ryan said that it’s been great to learn so much about the national sports of Ireland and that he is looking forward to following Gaelic football and hurling in the states.
Drama was after dinner and both Edel and Levi said that the students are making great progress on preparations for their drama presentations next Friday.  The students have been busy researching their assigned Irish historical figures, while writing preliminary scripts.  The drama presentations should be very enjoyable, said Angie.  She always looks forward to the creativity from the students.
Dance followed drama and Edel mentioned how amazed she is by the students’ enthusiasm.  While they might not be ready for Riverdance, they are definitely picking up the fundamentals of a jig and reel very quickly.  
On Friday night for an evening activity, students had the option of going to the movies at the Liffey Valley Shopping Center-across the road from King’s Hospital.  Many of the students saw Transformers 2 in 3D.  Many of the boys enjoyed the movie and said that it was better than the first Transformers.  Alyssa said it was entertaining, but recommended waiting until it comes out on DVD.  
All in all, it was a great day.  The students are loving Dublin!

title: Protected: Goodbye Waterford, Hello Dublin!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Thursday morning, we woke up early, finished packing, and loaded our suitcases onto the bus.  We said our goodbyes to Newtown Boarding School and Waterford and started our journey up the M9 to Dublin.  
We got to Dublin shortly after noon and ate our packed lunches in St. Stephen’s Green.  After lunch, Dan and Edel were thrilled to give the students a walking tour of Dublin to help students become familiar with the city.  They shared many points of interest with everyone during the stroll.  Down Kildare Street-pointing out the National Museum and Yeats’ Exhibit (Along with Lemon-Taryn’s favorite crepe shop.), over to Grafton Street-pointing out many Internet Cafes, restaurants, and shops-past Molly Malone and Trinity College, up Westmoreland Street-past Carroll’s, over O’Connell Bridge and the River Liffey-pointing out O’Connell statue, up to the GPO and Spire, back over the Ha’penny Bridge and into Temple Bar-and finally-past the actual Temple Bar where Edel used to work.  
Sallie said Dan and Edel’s tour was fantastic.  She said she was so overwhelmed, because there was so much to see and she wasn’t used to a big city.  Connor said that Dan was so funny pointing out everything, but that he was also very informative.  Ryan thinks that the tour will help him find his way around easier during his free time in Dublin.  Skoot said he loves Dublin.
Once we had gotten our bearings, it was time to go to King’s Hospital-where we would call home for the next nine days.  The rest of the night was spent exploring, relaxing, and settling into the new campus.  The student’s love how modern it is at King’s Hospital and many said they are enjoying all of the other student groups around.  It’s completely different than Newtown Boarding School and Waterford, but in a good way, said Connor.

title: Protected: Fun in Waterford!

It’s fun to listen to Irish people use slang in conversation and actually understand what they are talking about now, said Evan/Evo.  A few students have even been throwing the slang into their vocabulary and are looking forward to surprising a few friends back home with some new words.  
Irish American history was spent learning about the Kennedy’s.  Dan talked about JFK visiting Ireland and his famous speech in New Ross.  
After students spent the morning and early afternoon learning about more Irish culture and history, they had a little free time in Waterford or they could do the Celtic Key Chain’s Workshop with Taryn.  Then it was time for the GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association) Hurling Workshop. They learned the rules, practiced fundamental skills, and even were able to have a scrimmage with each other.  They loved it.

Mark commented on how fast the students picked up the sport.  He said it was the best group he’s seen in all his years of working with the ILE.   Mark was very impressed with Catherine, Kelsey, Sallie, and Tom’s performance.  They are naturally athletic with superb coordination. Later that evening, we did an Irish Life Experience Minute-To-Win-It.  Students were split into teams of three where they each had a minute to complete random tasks.

2)  Fore-Stack three golf balls on top of each other for three seconds.  A big shout out to Evo for being the only one to accomplish this challenging feat.  
3)  Oreotastic-Get an Oreo from your forehead to your mouth without using your hands.

5)  Chapstack-Stack three tubes of chapstick with chopsticks.  
6)  Don’t Blow the Joker-Blow a deck of cards off of a bottle without blowing off the bottom card of a Joker.  
Catherine said it was a fun activity, while Raizel/Prunes said that it was great for team bonding.  
The team of Alyssa/ABomb, Catherine/CMoney, and Sallie/Salli-nator were successful pulling off the win.  Just barely though.  It came down to a Penne Pick Up face-off between CMoney and Sasha Fierce.  It was a close match, but Catherine ended up pulling ahead on the sixth piece of penne.  Congrats girls!
The night ended with everyone packing up-getting ready to head to Dublin.  I can’t wait to head to the Big Smoke said Kelsey/Dunners!

title: Protected: A Bunch of Blarney and Put a Cork In It!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Tuesday marked our final tour day in Waterford to Cahir Castle, the Blarney Castle, Cork, and a quick stop in Youghal.  
Ireland’s largest and best preserved castles, Cahir is situated on a rocky island on the River Suir. Once the stronghold of the powerful Butler family, Cahir Castle became a feudal fantasy in a big way.  It’s a river-island site with moat, rocky foundations, massive walls, turrets and towers, defenses and dungeons.  Founded by Conor O’Brien in 1142, it was passed to the Butler family in 1375.  In 1599, it lost the arms race of its day when the Earl of Essex used cannons to shatter the walls.  
The castle was surrendered to Cromwell in 1650 without a struggle; its future usefulness may have discouraged the usual Cromwellian deconstruction.  It is largely intact and formidable still, and was restored in the 1840’s and again in the 1960’s when it came under state ownership.  
After a fifteen minute audio visual presentation and a quick tour, the real rewards came from a simple wandering through the remarkable survivor of Ireland’s medieval past.  Connor CassMan Cassidy said he really liked the tour and learned a lot.  Olivia/ODawg said that Cahir Castle was simply supercalifragilisticexpialidocious . 
Then we were off to Blarney.  Blarney Castle was built nearly six hundred years ago by one of Ireland’s greatest chieftains, Cormac MacCarthy, and has been attracting attention beyond Munster ever since.  Over the last few hundred years, millions have flocked to Blarney, making it a world landmark and one of Ireland’s greatest treasures.
The Blarney Stone is perched at the top of the 15th century castle, reached by a steep climb up a slippery spiral staircase.  On the battlements, you bend backwards over a long drop to kiss the stone.  Students tried not to think about the local lore of all the fluids that drench the stone other than saliva;).  In fact, Alyssa/ABomb said she wouldn’t kiss it because of all of the rumors.  So, she made a bet…  If Edel gave it a quick lick, than she would give it a little smooth.  ABomb lost the bet. 
The custom of kissing the stone is associated with Queen Elizabeth I.  She said to have invented the term to talk blarney-out of exasperation with Lord Blarney’s ability to talk endlessly without ever actually agreeing to her demands.  
The majority of the students made the trek up to receive the Gift of the Gab.  Kelly said it was a terrifying experience.  She was amazed by the perfect timing with weather though.  When they were climbing up the castle, it was pouring rain.  Then when they reached the top, the heavens cleared and the sun was shining once again.  Zoe/Zoe-inator said she was so proud of herself for kissing the Blarney Stone this time.  The last time she was in Ireland with her parents, she was too scared to kiss it.  
Students were able to explore the grounds and then do some shopping in the Blarney Woolen Mills.  Afterwards, we went to Cork.  We gave the students some money for dinner and they were able to pick a place where they wanted to eat-which was a real treat!  A few had Chinese, Italian, and some just settled for Supermac’s.  A few girls discovered even a larger Penney’s than the one in Waterford.  Happy Dayz!
Before we knew it, the day was coming to end and we had to head home.  We stopped in Youghal for a quick bathroom break.  Youghal is a beautiful seaside town and is most known for being the location where Moby Dick was filmed in 1956.  
It was a great day!

title: Protected: Fun with Limericks!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
This past week, drama was devoted to learning how to write limericks.  Edel and Levi assigned each student a specific Irish literary figure that they would need to research and write a limerick on.
A limerick is a five line poem written with one couplet and one triplet.  If a couplet is a two line rhymed poem, then a triplet would be a three line rhymed poem.  The rhyme pattern is a a b b a with lines one, two and five containing three beats and rhyming, and lines three and four having two beats and rhyming.  Some people say that the limerick was invented by soldiers returning from France to the Irish town of Limerick in the 1700’s.
Student’s work was judged yesterday and the best limerick is…,
There once was a man called Sam Beckett.
When writing a poem, he’ll totally wreck it!
Then one day ol’ Sammy got wise,
And he won the Nobel Lit. Prize.
But, when it comes to math he’ll say “Oh feck it!”
-Molly Fitzgerald, IL
Congratulations Molly!  Runner up was Fi.
There once was a writer,
His name was James Joyce.
Paris, Trieste, and Zurich were his spots of choice.
He lived how he pleased,
Though known as a sleaze.
He lives on in Ireland’s literary voice.
-Fiona Tomlin, CA
A few of the boys decided to write limericks about each other-all in harmless fun.  Just thought I would share these two for a laugh.
There once was a man from Kentucky,
Who was Irish, so thought he was lucky.
His hair was so red,
That everyone said,
He looked exactly like Chucky.
-Connor Cassidy, PR (Limerick about Evan)
There once was a man from Puerto Rico.
He was one badass crazy chico.
He wore stupid glasses,
So that everyone he passes,
Says “Oh my” what a freaking creepo.
-Evan McCullough, KY (Limerick about Connor)

Last night, the Irish Life Experience students participated in Edel’s exciting Waterford Scavenger Hunt.  
Students were divided into teams of six.  They were told that their first challenge would be to come up with a name and a cheer.  
Alyssa, Connor, Jenny, Raizel, Ryan, and Tom named their team the ILE-Intense Little Explorers and did a cheer to the theme song of Dora the Explorer.  It was hilarious.  
The ILE Babies, made up of Catherine, Evan, Fi, Kelly, Sallie, and Scout/Scoot did a superb cheer.  Sallie was their secret weapon, since she is a cheerleader and taught them her moves.  
Kels, MC, Molly, Olivia, Sasha and Zoe named themselves the Rockacons and definitely rocked the challenge.  
I’ll try to upload some of the student’s cheers to our ILE Fan Page on Facebook.  
They were then given two and a half hours to find and take pictures of certain items on a specific list around Waterford.  
A few items they had to find were:  A bag of Tayto crisps (Bonus points for a full bag, since Edel, Levi, and Taryn were hungry), a bank deposit slip, the best price for fish and chips in town, a business card, a banana peel, a family recipe from a local resident, a phone number for guitar lessons, a sachet of salt, and a take out menu…  They were even told they had to find a leprechaun.  Teams definitely got creative, when Evan and Molly dressed up as leprechauns.  It was hilarious!
Some of the things they had to take a picture of were:  A person from the US (Not on the ILE), a sheep, a team member with the Gardai, a team member pumping a stranger’s gas, a team member with his or her doppelganger, the team hugging a lamppost, the team sharing one soda and everyone having their own straw, and the “green man” on the traffic lights.  
When students returned, Edel added up the points for each team.  Some got a few bonus points when they tried to bribe the judges with chocolate.  In the end, it was a very close score.  However, the ILE Babies pulled it off and won.  Congratulations Evan, Fi, Kelly, Sallie, and Scoot.  They will be receiving a wonderful prize.  
Everyone did a great job and it was amazing how much they came together in their groups to accomplish each task.  They had a lot of fun.
We ended the day with the movie, In the Name of the Father.  Based on a true story with actor Daniel Day-Lewis-it’s about a small time thief from Belfast, Gerry Conlon.  Conlon is falsely implicated in the IRA bombing of a pub that kills several people while he is in London.  Bullied by the British police, he and four of his friends are coerced into confessing their guilt.  Gerry’s father and other relatives in London are also implicated in the crime.  He spends fifteen years in prison with his father trying to prove his innocence with the help of a British attorney, Gareth Peirce.    
Many students said it was a great film, but thought it was depressing.  They are looking forward to a more uplifting movie for the 4th of July.

title: Protected: From Castles to Cashels
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello Irish Life Experience Families and Friends!  
Yesterday, we had the opportunity to travel to Kilkenny Castle and the Rock of Cashel.  The weather, AGAIN was in our favor.  The sun shone most of the day and we were only caught in a few sprinkles of showers.  It was gorgeous for the majority of the tour and we couldn’t have lucked out more.  
We started the day with a tour of Kilkenny Castle.  The Castle stands dramatically on a strategic height that commands a crossing on the River Nore and dominates Kilkenny City.  Over the eight centuries of its existence, many additions and alterations have been made to the fabric of the building, making Kilkenny Castle today a complex structure of various architectural styles.  Scout said his favorite room of Kilkenny Castle was the Picture Gallery.  He especially thought the fireplace was interesting with all of the intricate designs.  
The original Anglo-Norman stone castle was built for William Marshal, 4th Earl of Pembroke (c.1146-1219) during the first decade of the  thirteenth century.  Kilkenny Castle later became the principal Irish residence of the powerful Butler family for almost 600 years.  The Butler ownership began when James (c.1360-1405), 3rd Earl of Ormond, purchased the castle in c.1391, and lasted until 1967 when Arthur, 6th Marquess of Ormonde (1893-1971), presented it to the people of Kilkenny in return for a token payment of £50.  Can you believe that???
Afterwards, we took some pictures in the garden and enjoyed our packed lunches on the lush green grounds.  Students were than able to wander around Kilkenny and had a blast meandering their way throughout the cobblestone streets shopping for souvenirs.  
A few hours later, we marched onwards to the Rock of Cashel.  For those of you who are unfamiliar with the Rock of Cashel-it’s huge, it’s complex, it’s iconic, and there is nothing like it anywhere else in the world!  It’s in the heart of Tipperary.  The Rock of Cashel-Carraig Phádraig, more formally known as St. Patrick’s Rock or the Cashel of the Kings.  Reputedly the site of the conversion of Aenghus the King of Munster by St. Patrick in the 5th century AD.  Long before the Norman invasion The Rock of Cashel was the seat of the High Kings of Munster, although there is little structural evidence of their time here.  Most of the buildings on the current site date from the 12th and 13th centuries when the rock was gifted to the Church.  The buildings represent both Hiberno-Romanseque and Germanic influences in their architecture.
The complex has a character of its own, unique and native, and is one of the most remarkable collections of Celtic art and medieval architecture to be found anywhere in Europe.
Students were able to explore the Rock and take some gorgeous pictures of views and the fortress itself.  It was spectacular.  Catherine thought Rock was so cool!

title: Protected: Wonderful Waterford
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Wednesday was the first day of classes for the Irish Life Experience.  Students woke up around 8 AM feeling refreshed and rejuvenated-anxious to start learning about Irish history and culture.  
After breakfast, they delved into Irish literature with Angie.  Angie shared the history of Irish literature with them and read a story by Frank O’Connor.  Tom said it was very interesting.
In Irish history, Dan talked about the Celts and Newgrange.   
Taryn taught the students about the geography and geology of Ireland in Irish studies.  She spiced up the class with a few jokes, which the students did not find quite as amusing;).  Joke:  How do you know an Irishman is having a good time?  Answer:  He’s Dublin over with laughter.  
In Irish American history with Dan, students shared their Irish roots and how their families came to America.  Thomas Meagher was the main focal point, as he was originally from Waterford and served as the Montana Governor after the Civil War.  Kelly was especially interested in him, since she has been able to trace her roots directly to him.  
Students had a quick lunch and then had their first opportunity to explore and wander around Waterford.  It was a pity, because it was the first time since we had been in Ireland that it was lashing down rain.  Being a fifteen minute walk into the city center, many students got drenched-even with a raincoat and an umbrella.  That didn’t stop them though.  Some of them found internet cafes, while others picked up cell phones.  A few became familiar with where the banks and post office were located.  Some girls even discovered the amazing discount store, Penney’s.  Ryan said you couldn’t go wrong with spending a day in Waterford.  Sallie echoed his enthusiasm.   
In the evening, students participated in drama and dance.  In drama they began working on limericks for the week of famous historical figures in Ireland.  The limericks will be judged and the winner will receive a prize.  In dance, the amazing Edel demonstrated the basics of 3’s and 7’s.  The students learned the steps very quickly with the help of Kelly and Raizel.  We were also lucky enough to have them show us their talent.  
At the end of of the evening, a group decided to play a game of soccer.  Alyssa said the impromptu game was a lot of fun.  Dan was also very impressed with Sasha.  He said she was a rock in the fence and had some great plays.  All in all, it was a fantastic day.

title: Protected: Fáilte to Ireland!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello Irish Life Experience Families and Friends,
Just a quick update on Tuesday’s events.  After we met Edel and Dan at Dublin Airport, we gathered our belongings and hopped on our lovely Barton’s coach that would take us to Waterford.  Edel pointed out things of interest along the way.  We even passed by her parent’s house and the students were excited to see the amount of cows her family owned.  Along the route, we stopped for a picnic of ham and veggie sandwiches in Glendalough-which means Valley of the Two Lakes.  Some people believe this is one of the most beautiful corners of Ireland and the epitome of the kind of rugged, romantic Ireland most people are familiar with when they think of the country.  The students were thrilled to learn that this is where part of the movie, PS I Love You was filmed.  Well, mainly the girls, since it’s somewhat of a chick flique.  
The substantial remains of Glendalough’s monastic settlement are impressive.  However, the real draw is the splendid setting of two dark and mysterious lakes tucked into a deep valley that is covered by a forest.  It is a deeply tranquil and spiritual place.  The students were able to stretch their legs and get some fresh air, which helped them recover from their jet leg.  Dan gave a fantastic tour of the monastery settlement and the 10th-century round tower.  A few students even stretched their arms around the tower to connect with one another, which supposedly brings good luck according to an Irish legend.  They walked around the surrounding graveyard, snapped pictures of the Celtic crosses, and took a stroll around the Lower Lake for some exercise.  A few of them skipped stones into the lake.  Evan had a stone that skipped 15 times-very impressive.  
Trying to fight off the exhaustion, we proceeded to travel down to Newtown Boarding School in Waterford.  We eventually got to our new home for the next ten days, where Angie joined us.  Angie gave the students a tour of campus.  They were then able to settle into their dorms and get freshened up.  We had tea shortly after, followed by a brief orientation.  Getting-to-Know-You Icebreakers was next, which was a lot of fun.  We learned some great facts about each other…  That Alyssa shaved her head to raise money for kids with cancer, that Fiona has been to seven different countries, that Sasha was hit in the face with a pickaxe when she was four, and that Tom won third place two years in a row for log rolling competitions.  We even attempted a human knot and were almost successful.  We managed to keep the students up until around 9 PM and most of them fell asleep immediately when their heads hit the pillow.  It was a quiet night.
Needless to say, it was a great start to the program.  The weather was even in our favor as we didn’t see any rain and basked in the sun for the majority of the day.  More to come…

title: Protected: Slán Agat USA!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello ILE Families and Friends!
Just a quick update on our very long travel day to Ireland.  Monday, the 27th, marked the departure of the 2011 Irish Life Experience.  It was an exciting time!  The day began around 10:30 AM, when Levi-our wonderful ILE Counselor, met Alyssa and Molly coming in from Chicago on their connecting flight.  Shortly thereafter, a few more students started arriving from California, Florida, Kentucky, Puerto Rico, and Washington.  Since our Aer Lingus flight didn’t depart until 9:40 PM, students had plenty of time for introductions and to explore and become familiar with Terminal 4 at JFK International Airport.  A few of them listened to their iPods, played card games, and read their books.  Many of them checked out Duty Free and got any last minute essentials they might have forgotten to pack.  They also got their fill on the American comfort food of Kentucky Fried Chicken, McDonald’s, and S’Barro, before they would enjoy the delicious Irish cuisine…, of potatoes:).
Levi said it was a very long day, but ran smoothly.  In fact, it was probably the easiest departure day we have ever had from JFK in the history of the ILE.  Sallie, coming from Montana, was the only flight delay.  However, she arrived with quite a lot of time to spare.  It was her first time on a plane, and she said she loved the experience.  She said it wasn’t as bad as she thought.  
Local students and families started to arrive around 5-6 PM.  They were met by Andrew, Levi, and Taryn, where they signed-in with the Irish Life Experience, received their T-Shirts and Tourism Ireland goodie bags.  A quick shout out to Andrew from Tenon Tours, who was kind enough to volunteer his time to help meet students from their connecting flights.  We all wished you could have joined us in Ireland.  Maybe next summer.  We eventually were allowed to check-in with Aer Lingus and before we knew it, it was time to go through Security and board our plane to the Emerald Isle.  Parents asked last minute questions and said their final good-byes, before we were able to capture a picture of the group.  No tears were shed and students were filled with a lot of excitement about the adventure they were about to embark upon.  Kelly said it was fun to meet everyone.  Jenny added it was similar to the terrifying exhilaration you get when you are on a roller coaster-a big ball of nerves.  
We breezed through Security and boarded EI 108, direct to Dublin.  The ILE occupied the back of the plane, got settled in their seats, and relaxed with a great selection of movies for the six hour journey across the pond.  Students were exhausted from their travel day, so quite a few of them got some much needed shut eye.
