title: Helpful Advice from 2010 Alumna, Sydney Alexander!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Dear 2011 ILE’ers,
Congratulations on becoming part of the Irish Life Experience Program.  It is coming up pretty quickly and I hope you are all excited.  I am very excited for you.  You are about to venture on a life changing journey.  You will soon discover a whole new world while also discovering yourself.  You will be invited to step outside your comfort zone, try new things, and challenge yourself.  You are about to discover who you really are and the change will touch your life for the better.  This journey to Ireland will mean so much more to you than you can even imagine at the moment.  In order to enjoy the fullness of the Irish Life Experience there are a few things you should keep in mind.
First off, do not be afraid.  I know that stepping out into the world on your own can be nerve wracking.  I’m a tiny Kansas girl who had barely stepped foot outside the Midwest-let alone the US, before my trip to Ireland.  Believe me, I know that it can be a little on the uneasy side, but I promise you that you have nothing to worry about.  Let go of all your fears and trust in those around you.  They will become your new family.  Taryn and all the ILE Staff are some of my favorite people in the world.  You will be in good hands.  Trust in them.  Confide in them.  They will take care of you and become some of your greatest friends.  If you have any worries at all-they will gladly take the weight off your shoulders.
Along with letting go of your fears and trusting in those around you comes the ability to keep an open mind.  Without an open mind, your time in Ireland will not be as impactful as it should.  Experience all you can on your journey.  Open up to all that surrounds you and absorb it all.  Live entirely in the moment.  Embrace the sounds, smells, and feel of Ireland.  Every second will be special.  You will cherish even the ordinary moments of this extraordinary journey.
Make sure you take lots of pictures.  Talk to everyone you meet.  Experience the culture.  Buy keepsakes.  Enjoy every second.  Cherish the people you are with and create memories that will live with you forever.  And at the end of the day be sure to write it all down in a journal.  This journal will become one of your most cherished possessions from the trip.  Write down all that you experienced and every emotion that ran through your body.  Write down the big events and the minor things that happened in the day.  You will be grateful to remember it in every detail.  I read through my journal often and I cherish the memories it holds.  At the end of our journey, I even had everyone write a note in the back of my journal.  It is the greatest “souvenir” from my trip.
Good Luck on your journey and I wish you all the best.  Make the most of it and enjoy every moment, as it will come to an end way too fast.  I wish I was joining this year for I would LOVE to go back again.  Be sure to start packing now so that you do not forget anything.  Be prepared for it all.  Make sure to send lots of postcards, especially to those in your life who have given you this wonderful opportunity.  You are very blessed.  Have a wonderful trip!
Sincerely,
Sydney Alexander

title: Helpful Advice from ILE 2010 Alumnus, PK Creedon!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello 2011 ILE’ers!
You are all about to embark on one of the greatest adventures of your lifetime:  Exploring the Emerald Isle!  I’m PK Creedon and I had the pleasure of traveling all over Ireland last summer with the Irish Life Experience.  I am completely jealous because I wish I was going back with you guys again!  I wanted to provide a couple packing tips and suggestions before you guys depart in a few short weeks!
1.  Have fun.  Do not let any little things spoil the short time you all have there!  It goes by so quick!
2.  Bring an open mind.  When consuming food-it may not all taste particularly delicious, but it helps you become more acclimated to their culture and it is better for you, too!
3.  Do NOT over pack.  Your suitcase will literally double in size after the first week of souvenir shopping.
4.  You will hit souvenir shop upon souvenir shop.  Only buy things you LOVE.
5.  Visit an Internet Café once or twice to update friends and family back home.  They are really easy to find!
6.  Bring car ride games!  Boggle, Bananagrams, a deck of cards, or Catch Phrase (But don’t forget to take the batteries out of that game-otherwise it will sound like a bomb is going off on the plane if it goes off and you might lose your life).  We spent the majority of our down time tossing a frisbee or playing a ton of different card games!
7.  Possibly weigh your luggage ahead of time so you have a general idea if you will have to pay extra money for your suitcase.  It may be cheaper and smarter to bring two suitcases instead of paying for one that is over weight.
8.  Bring a rain jacket and umbrella.  The weather was beautiful last summer, but rain is sporadic.
9.  Tell your parents to not miss you too much!  Mine were always checking the ILE Blog!  Taryn does a great job of updating them on everything!
RULE NUMBER 10.  Sing on the bus rides!  Take a bagillion photos!  Laugh until you cry!  Cry until you laugh!  Don’t miss home too much!  It’s only a month and the people you’re traveling with will become family!  Have a blast!

title: Protected: Introducing Levi Morgan-Your 2011 Male Counselor

content_raw: Hello everybody!  My name is Levi Morgan and I am very thrilled to be a Counselor for the Irish Life Experience this summer. I studied History and Comparative Politics at Knox College in Galesburg, Illionois-graduating in 2007. It was one of the best and most rewarding experiences of my life.  When I returned home, I took a job with a railroad with an eventual plan to return to school.  In 2009, I got that chance and I returned to Knox to become a teacher.  I am now certified and am currently looking for a High School Social Studies classroom to call my own!  Growing up in a small Illinois town, I did not have much regular exposure to other cultures, but the people I met in college and while traveling taught me how great it can be to learn and appreciate new ways of living.  I am looking forward to meeting you all this summer and experiencing the wonders of Ireland together!

title: Ann Hennessey Memorial Fund
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Three years ago, the world lost a beautiful soul.  Our dear friend, Ann Hennessey, of Morristown, New Jersey, passed away on March 30th, 2011 after battling a brief illness.
Ann was a devoted wife, a loving grandmother and mother, and a cherished friend.  She had many talents.  She was a dedicated educator, a devout volunteer, and a successful business woman.  She was a breath of fresh air and simply a joy to be around.  She always greeted you with open arms and a welcoming smile.  She was truly an inspiration to many.  She constantly gave her life to others, without expecting anything in return.  The lives she touched and the impact she made is profound.  She was truly selfless.
Ann never strayed too far from home.  She enjoyed cultivating her treasured garden.  She was a nurturer and her garden was her labor of love.  When she wasn’t tending to her flowers, she embraced spending time with her family-which was her true adoration.  She loved sharing stories of her recent travels to visit her children and showing pictures of her grandchildren.  Her eyes would magically sparkle when she talked about them.  Her family was her life.
Ann’s warm and gracious spirit will be missed and the world won’t be quite as bright without her glowing radiance.  Ann left footprints on the hearts of all she came in contact with, and their lives will never be the same.
Ann was very passionate about Irish culture, as her mother hailed from Co. Carlow, Ireland.  Being Irish and the incredible teacher that she was, we thought it only be appropriate to honor Ann with a Memorial Fund for the Irish Life Experience.  All of the money raised will go directly to a student/s who would otherwise not have the means to attend this amazing program.
We will never forget you Ann!  Please help us pay tribute to this remarkable woman!
May the road rise up to meet you.
May the wind be ever at your back.
May the sun shine warm upon your face,
And the rain fall softly on your fields.
And until we meet again, May God hold
you in the hollow of his hand.

title: Happy St. Patrick’s Day from Feis America!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
“In life, as in dance, grace glides on blistered feet.”
One of my favorite jobs at Feis America is getting to spend time with the three generations who often accompany competitive Irish dancers to events.  There are not many athletic pursuits or pastimes that draw extended families together and it’s worth celebrating!
It follows, of course, that the month of March-with dance-outs, parades and performances all across North America-is also a celebration which extends to several generations and friends, too.  Reunions take place, lost souls are honored, stories are exchanged, babies are introduced and photos are shared almost instantly.
The connection we Irish Americans have with one another is not unique; other cultures are known for their family gatherings too.  What continues to astound me, however, is the connection we Irish Americans have with Ireland herself.  The desire of North American dance families to get to the All Ireland Championships or Oireachtas Rince na Cruinne (World Championships) means a journey back ‘home,’ even if the family is two or three generations removed from an Irish birthplace!
The opportunity to study, travel and explore Irish culture is a goal of nearly every dancer and their non-dancing siblings I meet.  I encourage families to make the most of any trip to Ireland to include a roadtrip ‘off the beaten path.’
The Irish Life Experience is a tremendous opportunity to reinforce that connection with Ireland, while promoting our American ties there on the Emerald Isle.
For all of our great grandparents or grandparents who emigrated and could never look back, your experience in Ireland honors the sentiment and beauty of what they left behind to make a better life.
Your only obligation is to bring back stories to inspire a new generation to make the journey themselves!
Happy Saint Patrick’s Day from North America’s favorite Irish dancing magazine, Feis America!
***Thank you so much Kathleen for your wonderful article!  Kathleen O’Reilly-Wild is the founding publisher and editor in chief of the consumer niche magazine, Feis America, published in Connecticut.  Feis America is a bi-monthly full color celebration of everything related to Irish dance in North America and beyond and serves a market of more than 150,000 Irish dance students and their teachers, parents, families and fans with articles, competition followups, results, health, adult Irish dancing, first feis, sights, sounds, feis music, feis world, and directory of trusted events and resources for Irish dance enthusiasts around the world.  If you would like more information or would like to subscribe to Feis America, visit their website:  www.feisamerica.com, become a fan on Facebook, and follow them on Twitter.***

title: Kiss Me, I’m Irish!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Irish Life Experience Friend and Blogger, Jennifer Holloway from Portland, Oregon, shares how she will celebrate the St. Patrick’s Day spirit next week.
  My Irish descendants set sail for America in 1811.  If I had known that more than just a few years ago, I might own a “Kiss Me, I’m Irish” T-Shirt along with the rest of the proud Irish Americans.  Unfortunately, the celebration of my Irish heritage goes about as far as the Lucky Charms I had for breakfast this morning-true story.  I honestly forgot to wear green on St. Patrick’s Day last year!  This year, however, I’ll celebrate St. Patrick’s Day the way it should be done.  My book club happens to be meeting on March 17th.  Our hostess is making corned beef, Irish soda bread, potatoes, and veggies.  I’ve signed up for dessert and although I’m undecided on what to make, the list of ingredients will likely include Bailey’s.  We even read Frank McCourt’s “Angela’s Ashes” to keep with the Irish theme. No, we didn’t, but the rest of it is true!  The only thing Irish about our book is that you can buy it in Ireland-along with anywhere else in the world.  Ah well…, it will still be an excellent celebration.
Out of curiosity, I did some research to learn more about Saint Patrick.  As it turns out, facts about his life vary depending upon the source.  There are some pieces most scholars accept to be true, though.  According to Coilin Owens, Irish literature expert at George Mason University, Saint Patrick lived between 432-461 A.D.  At 16, he was kidnapped from the Roman British Isles and sold into slavery in Ireland. Saint Patrick turned to religion for solace and after six years he escaped.  While back in his homeland, Patrick decided to become a priest and then decided to return to Ireland after dreaming that the Irish people were calling him to convert them to Christianity.  He traveled back to Ireland as a Christian missionary and his mission in Ireland is said to have lasted for thirty years. Patrick died in the 5th century on March 17th–The day we continue to celebrate this patron saint of Ireland with jovial parades, Irish festivals, and all things green-even the beer…  An American addition, of course.
Why not extend the celebration?  March 5th–14th is Seachtain na Gaeilge, an international celebration of the Irish language.  I’ll celebrate by attempting to use a few new phrases:  Tá tinneas cinn orm (I have a headache) and An bhfuil spúnóg agat? (Do you have a spoon?)  I didn’t say they were necessarily useful phrases.  Perhaps I’ll watch a movie or two with some of the worst fake Irish accents out there-think Julia Roberts in “Mary Reilly” or Tom Cruise in “Far and Away”.  Sadly, they’re much better than any attempt I could make!  Whatever the celebration includes, I’ll put more effort into St. Patrick’s Day than in years past.  I may even have to buy a new T-Shirt for the occasion…  “Kiss me, I’m Irish!”
***Thank you Jennifer.  The Irish Life Experience appreciates you and looks forward to more of your posts.***

title: Trip of a Lifetime
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Irish Life Experience Friend, Jennifer Holloway from Portland, Oregon, shares her experience studying abroad in London.  While it wasn’t the Emerald Isle she studied in, we won’t discriminate against the important message she sends to all students.  Ha!  Thank you Jenny for giving us a special glimpse into your adventure abroad.  
Spring semester of my Junior year I decided to study abroad.  I went for all of the reasons you’re supposed to study abroad…  I wanted to broaden my perspective, see the world, and (let’s be honest) I knew it would look fantastic on any graduate school and employment application down the road.  Our coursework immersed us in British theater, art, architecture, government and literature.  Instead of just reading about it, though, we visited castles, attended plays, and toured museums for truly experiential learning.  I’d never been so excited about learning in all my life!
I knew I would learn about British history, current events, and important people and places.  What I didn’t expect was that they would forever be associated with great memories of the friendships I made and the experiences I had there.  I’ll never see a picture of former Prime Minister Tony Blair without being reminded of the friend who had a raging crush on him!  Dame Judi Dench will always be one of my favorite actresses ever since I saw her in a play called “Amy’s View.”  The British Museum houses an enormous collection of art and artifacts.  It’s also the place where my friends and I took pictures alongside famous statues (imitating their poses, of course) and I stared utterly fascinated at Lindow Man, the 1st century AD bog body.  To this day, I can’t have a cup of loose leaf tea without remembering how good it tasted when my host family made it and how terrible it was when I did!  I was lucky enough to be able to travel to other places in Europe as well.  I ate mystery food in Munich (sadly, none of us spoke German), sunbathed in Nice, and learned to Salsa in Barcelona.  Everything about my study abroad experience was unforgettable and remains the highlight of my college years.
There are a thousand reasons why young people should study abroad.  For me, the most important one is that it will never again be the experience it can be at that age.  There’s just something about the immediate acceptance into the constant culture of young travelers and the excitement of experiencing it all for the first time together that sets it apart from travel later in life.  There’s this hunger to see it all (on a dime, of course) and there are lifelong friendships to be formed along the way with people from all over the world.  It’s been 12 years and I’m still in touch with the friends I made in England and the Americans I traveled with.  I’m also still terrible at making loose leaf tea!  It will never taste as good as it does in London.
Steinbeck had it right when he said “we do not take a trip; a trip takes us.”  I’m so thankful that one took me when it did.

title: Protected: Connemara at its Best!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
The Irish Life Experience went to Dan O’Hara’s Heritage Center on Tuesday for a few hours and left with many memories to treasure.
The Dan O’Hara Heritage Center is built on the site of the original cottage home of Dan from Connemara-renowned in the popular Irish Ballad all over the world.
Along with his wife and seven children, Dan lived in this tiny cottage and the family were self-sufficient even in times when poverty stalked most other areas of Ireland in the early 1840’s.
On the eight acre farm the O’Hara family had their own crops, they had the usual array of farm animals as well as ducks and hens around the farmyard.
The turf for the fire was also cut in the local bog by Dan, and in the flickering firelight of Dan O’Hara’s kitchen many a marriage stemmed from relationships developing into romance at the Ceili dances in this Connemara kitchen which was the the Ballroom of Romance of another era.
But the tranquillity was suddenly shattered by the dreaded “battering ram” and the landlord who laid his old home low when Dan was unable to pay the exorbitant rent demanded by his superiors after it was discovered he had modernized his little home in 1845.
Dan, his wife and seven young children had to abandon their homeland and work for their passage on an emigrant ship bound for New York.  Sadly his wife and three of their children died on that terrible journey.
With his four children fostered out to American families, Dan was a broken man selling matches on the streets of New York-a far cry from the tranquillity that his family had enjoyed in scenic Connemara.
Now the cottage has been restored to it’s past glory.  Irish Life Experience students were invited to step back into the past in this traditional Dan O’Hara cottage and the music, merriment and memories of another era came floating back in their mind’s eye.
Martin, our wonderful host, took the students on a tractor ride to take in gorgeous views of the Connemara, showed them how to cut turf, told them about Dan O’Hara, and challenged them to a tug-a-war.  Students even had a horseshoe throwing contest, and Hannah won the grand prize of delicious Irish chocolates.  
Our next stop, was a brief photo opportunity at Kylemore Abbey.  Kylemore is a Benedictine monastery founded in 1920 on the grounds of Kylemore Castle.  The abbey was founded for Benedictine Nuns who fled Belgium in World War I.
Prior to Kylemore becoming an Abbey, it was built as a Castle and private home for the family of Mitchell Henry, a wealthy politician from Manchester, England who was also MP for Galway County from 1871 to 1885.  
The Castle covered approximately 40,000 square feet with over 70 rooms and the principal wall was two to three feet thick.  The facade measured 142 feet in length and is made of granite brought from Dalkey by sea to Letterfrack and limestone from Ballinasloe.  There were 33 bedrooms, 4 bathrooms, 4 sitting rooms, ballroom, billard room, library, study, school room, smoking room, gun room and various offices and domestic staff residences for the butler, cook, housekeeper and other servants.
In 1920, Kylemore became an Abbey and is the oldest of the Irish Benedictine Abbeys. The Community of nuns, who have resided here for 189 years, have a long history stretching back almost three hundred and forty years.  Founded in Ypres, Belgium, in 1665, the purpose of the Abbey at Ypres was to provide an education and religious community for Irish women during times of persecution here in Ireland.  Down through the centuries, Ypres Abbey attracted the daughters of the Irish nobility, both as students and postulants, and enjoyed the patronage of many influential Irish families living in exile.
Here the nuns opened an international boarding school and established a day school for local girls, which closed in June 2010.  Since the 70’s, the Benedictine Community have opened their Abbey and Estate to the public and now Kylemore has become known as a must see when visiting the West of Ireland.  
Before heading back to Galway, we stopped at the Connemara Marble Factory, where students were able to get a quick tour and pick up a few last minute souvenirs.  
It was a great day for the ILE!

title: Protected: Aran-rific!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
One of the highlights of the Irish Life Experience is a trip to the Aran Islands.  The Aran Islands are a group of three islands located at the mouth of Galway Bay.  From west to east they are: Inishmore, Inishmaan, and Inisheer and Irish is the main spoken language on all three islands.
On Monday, we set sail from Rossaveal for a fun filled day of biking around the island of Inishmore-the largest of the three islands.  We arrived around 10:30 AM and rented bikes for all of the students.  From there, everyone was able to enjoy their packed lunches and explore the island on their own-all by nine miles in length and two miles in width.  It rained for the first hour we were on the island, but once again the skies opened up and the sun once shone down upon the Irish Life Experience.  
The islands’ geology is mainly karst limestone and is thus closely related to the Burren.  Huge boulders up to 80 feet above the sea at parts of the west facing cliffs have been shown not to be glacial erratics as originally believed, but rather as an extreme form of storm beach, cast there by giant waves that occur on average once per century.
A lacework of ancient stone walls enfolds all three islands to contain local livestock.  Also found are early clocháns-dry-stone beehive huts from the early-Christian period.  Enda of Aran founded the first true Irish Monastery near Killeany.  In time there were a dozen monasteries on Inishmore alone.  Many Irish saints had some connection with Aran.  St. Brendan was blessed for his voyage there, Jarlath of Tuam, Finnian of Clonard, and St. Columba called it the “Sun of the West.”
Since the islands were first populated in larger numbers, probably at the time of the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland in the mid 17th century, when the Catholic population of Ireland had the choice of going “to hell or to Connaght,” many fled to the numerous islands off the west coast of Ireland.  There they adapted themselves to the raw climatic conditions, developing a survival system of total self-sufficiency.  Their methods included mixing layers of sand and seaweed on top of rocks to create fertile soil, a technique used to grow potatoes and other vegetables.  The same seaweed method also provided grazing grass within stone-wall enclosures for cattle and sheep, which in turn provided wool and yarn to make handwoven trousers, skirts and jackets, hand-knitted sweaters, shawls, caps, and hide shoes.  The islanders also constructed unique boats for fishing, building their thatched cottages from the materials available or trading with the mainland.
Many Irish Life Experience students went to Dún Aonghasa.  Dún Aonghasa is the most famous of several prehistoric forts on the Aran Islands.  It is located on the top of a 250 foot cliff and is an important archaeological site that also offers a spectacular view. It is not known when Dún Aonghasa was built, though it is now thought to date from the Iron Age.  It was probably originally constructed as a circular ringfort several hundred feet from the coast, its present precarious position being the result of centuries of coastal erosion.
The fort consists of a series of four concentric walls of dry stone construction.  Surviving stonework is twelve feet wide at some points.  The original shape was presumably oval or D-shaped but parts of the cliff and fort have since collapsed into the sea.  Outside the third ring of walls lie a defensive system of stone slabs, known as a ‘Chevaux de frise,’ planted in an upright position in the ground and still largely well-preserved.  These ruins also feature a huge rectangular stone slab, the function of which is unknown.  Impressively large among prehistoric ruins, the outermost wall of Dún Aonghasa encloses an area of approximately 14 acres.  Although clearly defensible, the particular location of Dún Aonghasa suggests that its primary purpose was religious and ceremonial rather than military.  It may have been used for seasonal rites by the druids, perhaps involving the bonfires that could be seen from the mainland of Ireland.
Students soaked up the gorgeous views and cautiously laid close to the edge of the cliffs, inhaling the fresh Irish sea air.  Joe said it was more impressive and untouched than the Cliffs of Moher and Sydney said it was one of her favorite days of the whole program.  
On the three mile journey back to the village of Inishmore, students stopped at a beautiful beach to go swimming and collect shells, looked through a telescope at the seal colony vantage point, took pictures of donkeys and horses, picked flowers, and fixed chains on their bikes.  Eventually, everyone returned to the port, where they enjoyed banana and Nutella crepes as a treat.  Rough waters provided a fun trip back to the mainland, but students were able to get a bird’s eye view from sitting on top of the Aran ferry.  We arrived back to Gort na Coiribe, exhausted after an incredible experience and a few rosy cheeks.  It was simply a spectacular day!

title: Protected: The Beautiful Burren!
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello Irish Life Experience Families and Friends, I apologize for the delay in posts, but our last week in Ireland was very hectic-with very little time to blog.  However, I wanted to make sure I filled you in on the last five days of the most incredible Irish Life Experience summer.  
On Sunday, the 18th, the Irish Life Experience toured the Burren with our magnificent Brian Farrell of Burren Coaches.  The Burren, meaning “great rock” in Irish, is a karst-landscape region in northwest County Clare.  It is one of the largest karst landscapes in Europe, with layers of soluble bedrock-mainly limestone.  The region measures approximately 155 miles and is enclosed roughly within the circle made by the villages Ballyvaughan, Corofin, Kilfenora, Kinvara, Lisdoonvarna, and Tubber.  It is bounded by the Atlantic and Galway Bay on the west and north, respectively.
During counter-guerilla operations in the Burren during 1651-52, Edmund Ludlow stated, “The Burren is a country where there is not enough water to drown a man, wood enough to hang one, nor earth enough to bury him…, and yet their cattle are very fat; for the grass growing in turfs of earth, of two or three foot square, that lie between the rocks, which are of limestone, is very sweet and nourishing.” 
Brian Farrell is originally from Ballyvaughn, so he is very knowledgeable of the area.  He educated the students about the limestone pavements with crisscrossing cracks known as “grikes,” leaving isolated rocks called “clints.”  He also told the students, even though the Burren is mainly limestone, they better not take it for granite;).  Ha!  
Before our tour began, we stopped in Ballyvaughn to pick up Brian’s three adorable children Eoghan, Mia, and Shona, who you will see in a few of the pictures.  
Brian’s first stop on the tour was the Poulnabrone Dolmen-meaning hole of sorrows.  It is a portal tomb dating back to the Neolithic period, probably between 4200 BC to 2900 BC.  The dolmen consists of a twelve-foot, thin, slab-like, tabular capstone supported by two slender portal stones, which lift the capstone six feet from the ground, creating a chamber in a thirty foot low cairn.  The cairn helped stabilize the tomb, and would have been much higher originally. 
A crack was discovered in the eastern portal stone in 1985.  Following the resulting collapse, the dolmen was dismantled, and the cracked stone was replaced. Excavations during this time found that between 16 and 22 adults and 6 children were buried under the monument.  Personal items buried with the dead included a polished stone axe, a bone pendant, quartz crystals, weapons and pottery.  In the Bronze Age, around 1700BC, a newborn baby was buried in the portico, just outside the entrance.  With its dominating presence on the limestone landscape of the Burren, the tomb was likely a centre for ceremony and ritual until well into the Celtic period.  
The ILE students were able to take plenty of pictures of the Poulnabrone Dolmen and also walk around the site ten times counter clockwise, as Irish legend states after doing so-they will have the gift of fertility.
Our next stop was for a packed lunch in Kilfenora.  Kilfenora means Church of the Fertile Hillside or Church of the White Brow.  Students were able to enjoy their crisps, sandwiches, and sweets-while taking a gander by Kilfenora Cathedral.  The Cathedral dates back from the 12th Century and there are three impressive high crosses on the site.  Kilfenora is also the village where much of the filming of the Irish sitcom Father Ted took place.  
After lunch and a few 99’s, we stopped at St. Brigid’s Well in Liscannor.  St. Brigid’s Well is found near the Cliffs of Moher and is in an area of great scenic beauty.   Behind the well on a higher level to which steps lead, is an ancient cemetery in which the Uí Bhrian, the Kings of Dál gCais, are buried.  There is a large cross here and a circular path around it.  Part of the Rite of the Holy Well is performed in this area known as the ‘Ula Uachtarach’ or upper sanctuary.
The Well itself is in the lower ground, the ‘Ula íochtarach’ or lower sanctuary, enclosed in a little house full of votive offerings such as holy pictures, medals, and rosaries left by visitors.  
This site has a particularly mysterious atmosphere which may be felt at once by visitors, as they enter the grove and hear the gentle lapping of the water in the background.  
The Liscannor Well was regarded as a place of healing and crutches were left there as an indication that a pilgrim had been cured through the intercession of the Blessed Brigid.  A wandering poet describes his visit to the well, “On St Brigid’s Eve, as night fell, My mother and I went to Saint Brigid’s Well, Where the candles do burn and the great walls do shine on the graves of the dead and the vaults of O’Brien.”
It was a very meaningful and peaceful time for the ILE students.  A few left behind cherished items of important people that had passed away.  It was very touching.  
From St. Brigid’s Well, we went around the corner to the Cliffs of Moher.  The Cliffs of Moher rank as one of the most popular tourist destinations in Ireland and topped the list of attractions in 2009 by drawing almost one million visitors.  The Cliffs rise 394 feet above the Atlantic Ocean at Hag’s Head and reach their maximum height of 702 feet just north of O’Brien’s Tower.  
O’Brien’s Tower is a round stone tower at the approximate midpoint of the cliffs.  It was built by Sir Cornelius O’Brien, a descendant of Ireland’s High King Brian Boru, in order to impress female visitors.  Legend states that if you place your forehead and hands on O’Brien’s Tower and hum for ten seconds, you will be blessed with wealth for the rest of your life.  Needless to say, the sounds of many ILE students humming could be heard at the Cliffs this day.  
Students also learned that the Princess Bride and Harry Potter and the Half Blood Prince movies were filmed at the Cliffs of Moher.  Luckily is was a gorgeous day and the students were able to get plenty of incredible pictures of the beautiful scenery.  Awe-inspiring indeed! 
On our way home, we stopped for a few more photo opportunities and the students were introduced to Father Ted on DVD.  It was another brilliant day for the Irish Life Experience.  Clara said, “The Burren is rich with historical and archaeological sites.  I can’t wait to return.”  
Once back to Gort na Coiribe, the menus consisted mainly of pizzas and an early bedtime in preparation for our Aran Island’s journey the next day.

title: Protected: Carrick-a-rede Craic
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Next on the Irish Life Experience agenda was Carrick-a-rede Rope Bridge.  
Carrick-a-Rede Rope Bridge is a rope suspension bridge near Ballintoy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland.  The bridge links the mainland to the tiny Carrick Island.  The site is owned and maintained by the National Trust, spans sixty-five feet and is ninety-eight feet above the rocks below.  Today the bridge is mainly a tourist attraction, with 247,000 visitors in 2009.  
Carrick-a-rede means “rock in the road.”  It is thought salmon fishermen have been erecting bridges to the island for over 350 years. It has taken many forms.  In the 1970’s it featured only a single handrail and large gaps between the slats.  A version of the bridge, tested up to ten tonnes, was built with the help of local climbers and abseilers in 2000.  A subsequent design was engineered in 2004 and offers visitors and fishermen alike a much safer passage to the island. The current wire rope and Douglas fir bridge was made by Heyn Construction in Belfast and erected early in 2008 at a cost of over £16,000.  Although no one has fallen off the bridge, there have been many instances where visitors, unable to face the walk back across the bridge, have had to be taken off the island by boat.
Crossing the bridge is not for the faint of heart and there were definitely a few weak knees at the thought.  The area is exceptional in natural beauty with stunning views of Rathlin Island and Scotland.  Simply breathtaking!
A special shout out to Katie.  She sprained her ankle during the Rugby Workshop and has been such a trooper lately.  She had crutches for two days and managed to hop her way and get piggy back rides from friends and ILE Staff-just so she could see the Giant’s Causeway and Carrick-a-Rede Rope Bridge.  What a champ!  She didn’t even complain once.
We finished our Northern Tour for the day with a stop at Ballycastle, just as it started to downpour.  The students each received a dinner stipend.  Fish and chips seemed to be the popular the popular choice on the menu for most of the ILE’ers.  
After dinner, we decided it was time to head back to Dublin, before it got too late.  During the next few hours, Angie serenaded us with a few tunes from ACDC.  The ILE Staff also treated the students to a few Michael Jackson tunes on their iPod’s.  We are just trying to groom the students for the many sing songs we will be having on the west coast during our Holidays.  We finally returned back to King’s Hospital in Dublin at 10:00 PM.  I don’t know how they did it-I was exhausted-but the students decided they had enough energy to go dance at the King’s Hospital Disco.  Amazing!
So…, this sums up our Thursday with the Irish Life Experience.  What a magnificent day!

title: Protected: Fionn mac Cumhaill-Legend or Truth?
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Since I have so many gorgeous pictures of our incredible Irish Life Experience students from our excursion up North on Thursday, I decided to treat you to three separate posts.  
After our fantastic tour of Belfast, we headed even further north along the Antrim Coast.  Another hour and a half on the road, before we arrived at the Giant’s Causeway.  Here enjoyed our packed lunch in each other’s company.  The weather was in our favor, as once again the clouds pushed away and the sun warmed our cheeks.  I think the 2010 ILE’ers are our good luck weather charms.  On full stomachs, we watched an audio visual on the history of the Causeway and let our food digest, before we went exploring and hiking, with our fearless leader-Angie guiding the way.     
The Giant’s Causeway is an area of roughly 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, the result of an ancient volcanic eruption.  In a 2005 poll of Radio Times readers, the Giant’s Causeway was named as the fourth greatest natural wonder in the United Kingdom.  The tops of the columns form stepping stones that lead from the cliff foot and disappear under the sea. Most of the columns are hexagonal, although there are also some with four, five, seven and eight sides.  The tallest are about 36 feet high, and the solidified lava in the cliffs is 70 feet thick in places.  
Some 50 to 60 million years ago, during the Paleogene period, Antrim was subject to intense volcanic activity, when highly fluid molten basalt intruded through chalk beds to form an extensive lava plateau.  As the lava cooled rapidly, contraction occurred.  While contraction in the vertical direction reduced the flow thickness, horizontal contraction could only be accommodated by cracking throughout the flow.  The size of the columns is primarily determined by the speed at which lava from a volcanic eruption cools. The extensive fracture network produced the distinctive columns seen today.  The basalts were originally part of a great volcanic plateau called the Thulean Plateau which formed during the Paleogene period.
While many people believe the geological interpretation of how the Giant’s Causeway was formed, Angie prefers the legend instead.  It is said that Irish warrior Fionn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool) built the Causeway to walk to Scotland to fight his Scottish counterpart Benandonner.  After seeing Benandonner’s great bulk, Fionn asked his wife to disguise him as the baby.  When Benandonner saw the size of the ‘infant’, he assumed the alleged father, Fionn, must be gigantic indeed.  Therefore, Benandonner fled home in terror, ripping up the Causeway in case he was followed by Fionn.  See…, isn’t the legend much more entertaining?
The ILE soaked in all of the gorgeous views at the Giant’s Causeway and many said it was their favorite place thus far.  We took many pictures by the Organ, Giant’s Boot, Giant’s Eyes, and the Shepherd’s Steps. 
Enjoy!

title: Protected: Prayers for Peace
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Thursday, the Irish Life Experience arose very early for an amazing tour to Belfast, the Giant’s Causeway, and Carrick-a-rede Rope Bridge.  With a 7:30 AM start to our long day, students settled in for the two hour bus trip to Belfast.  Many slept the whole way and listened to their iPod’s, while Taryn took some classic ILE sleeping pictures.  She has most of the students catching some “Z’s”, except for Dakota, Joe, and Savannah.  She is determined to get everyone by the end of the trip!
When we arrived to Belfast, we were met by Taxi Trax Black Taxi’s.  Our fantastic tour guides-Eddie, Joel, and Paul-took the Irish Life Experience students on a journey into the politics of Belfast from the late 1960’s to the Present Day and gave the students an insight into the conflict’s history.  They took time out to show us the famous wall murals throughout Belfast that conveyed the people’s culture, history, and politics.
We visited the Shankhill first-the Protestant area in West Belfast. Students were amazed to see the amount of Union Jacks and the very depictive murals here.  A few also noticed the remnants of bonfires from July 12th; the beginning of Marching Season in the North.  
From there, we went to a few memorials along the way, paying tribute to those who had innocently lost their lives during the Troubles.  
Our guides told the students about the Hunger Strikers and stopped at the Bobby Sands’ mural-taking time to honor him.  
We finished the tour on the Falls Road-the Catholic area of West Belfast.  The Falls and Shankhill Roads are still bisected with a high wall with gates that shut the one side off from the other at night.  Ironically, it is called the Peace Wall.  A few Irish Life Experience students left heartfelt messages behind on the Peace Wall, encouraging prayers and a hope for an end to the violence forever.  It was amazing to see the students share faith and a vision for peace on the once bloody battle grounds of the Troubles.  It was so moving!  “Peace, Not War,” wrote Clara.

title: Protected: Workshops Galore
author: tharrison
content_raw:
After visiting Áras an Uachtaráin on Wednesday, the Irish Life Experience students returned to King’s Hospital for an array of Irish workshops to fill the rest of their day.  
Angie first gave her Northern Ireland Workshop and talked about growing up in Belfast during the height of the Troubles.  She spoke very passionately about what she witnessed and gave the students a small peak into the history of the conflict.  It was a perfect time to talk about the North, since the ILE students were heading to Belfast and the Antrim Coast on Thursday.  She told the students how much progress and peace had been made in recent years.  “Angie’s Northern Ireland Workshop was very powerful and made me understand more about the Troubles that Northern Ireland has endured over the years,” said Hannah.  
Later that afternoon, Dan taught rugby.  Dan is a rugby coach at Terenure College in Dublin, so he has plenty of experience teaching the rules and techniques of the game.  He even had some of his former students come to the workshop to help the students practice and show them a few tricks of the trade.  He explained many passes and moves, before allowing the students to scrimmage against each other.  
With a few goals, rucks, scrums, and tackles, the ILE students picked up the sport very quickly.  While many seem to favor Gaelic football, they all enjoyed learning rugby-especially from Dan and his students.  A few mentioned they are interested in getting the National Irish Rugby Jersey and following the Irish Rugby Team in the US.  
Later that evening, a past teacher of the Irish Life Experience, graced us with her presence and taught an Advanced Irish Dancing and Tin Whistle Workshop to the ILE students.  Corinna O’Donoghue first demonstrated a special dancing routine to Hannah and Scarlett.  They worked very diligently for over an hour and managed to learn the steps to Corinna’s routine very quickly.  
Next was the impressive Tin Whistle Workshop.  Corinna taught the students a basic scale on a D Whistle-D, E, F, G, A, B, C-and then showed them how to play a polka and a slip jig.  Taryn was amazed by how fast the students learned the two tunes.  They are very musical.  Dakota and Katie were naturals at the instrument and both said they were going to try and learn a few more Irish tunes when they get home.  Thank you Corinna for your expertise;)!
Taryn is trying to convince the students to showcase their talents on the final night in Galway, so hopefully they will share their newfound Irish routines for their ILE friends.

title: Protected: The ILE and Tea at Áras an Uachtaráin
author: tharrison
content_raw:
On Wednesday, the Irish Life Experience received a very special invitation from the President of Ireland.  While President McAleese was away in Kerry for her holidays, she graciously opened her home to us and arranged a special tour for our students, complete with coffee, tea, and scones with jam.  Dressed in our Sunday’s best, we were greeted by the Secretary General to the President, Adrian O’Neill.  He welcomed us to Áras an Uachtaráin and to Ireland and expressed how proud he was to see American students taking such a strong interest and desire to learn about Irish culture.  He told the students it’s up to them to keep Irish culture alive in the US and hoped they would return to Ireland many more times in the future.  
After introductions and sipping on Bewley’s, Adrian’s assistant gave us a fantastic tour of the main floor of the President’s House.  
Áras an Uachtaráin has had a colourful history before becoming the Official Residence of the President of Ireland.  Built in 1751 and situated in the 1,752 acres of the Phoenix Park near Dublin, the original house was built by Park Ranger Nathaniel Clements.  By 1782 it had been acquired for use by the Viceroys who oversaw British rule in Ireland.  Clements received £25,000 for the house.
The house continued as the official residence of the Viceroys until 1922. For much of the period of Home Rule that followed it was the residence of the Governors General, the Crown’s representatives during the new dispensation.  In 1938 it became the Official Residence of the President of Ireland and has been used for that purpose since.
The ILE students saw four important rooms on the main floor of the President’s House.  The first was the State Dining Room.  The State Dining Room was built in 1849 for a visit by Queen Victoria.  The ILE students gathered and sat around a beautiful table, made in 1927.  The table, was formerly the Cabinet table in Leinster House and was brought to the Áras by Eamon de Valera in 1960.  The first meeting of new Governments is usually held around this table after Ministers have received their Seals of Office from the President.  Many important people in Ireland’s history sat around this table, so it was a special way for the ILE students to have a connection to Ireland’s past and present.  
The first President of Ireland, Dr. Douglas Hyde, lived in the house from 1938-1945.  In 1944, he decided to assemble a small collection of pictures and portraits representing significant people and events in the history of Ireland, and donated many of the works himself.  Of historical rather than artistic interest, the collection was at first displayed in the Council of State Room. Now portraits of past Presidents by contemporary Irish artists hang on the State Dining Room walls.
The second room we entered was the State Reception Room.  This room was formerly the ballroom and dates from 1802, just after the Act of Union.  
A beautiful handwoven carpet from Donegal is the focal point in the room, which you can see in the second picture. Its centerpiece depicts the Phoenix rising from the flames and the four heads on each corner replicate the riverine figures of James Gandon’s Custom House, which represent the principal rivers of Ireland.
The next room we entered was the Council of State Room.  It is part of the original house, built in 1751, and is now generally used as a reception room.  Originally a dining room, it had been fitted up as a billiard room in the 1840s.  Its coved plaster ceiling, part-gilded and unusual in Ireland, is attributed to Bartholomew Cramillion, who introduced this Rococo style into Irish plasterwork in the mid-18th century.  It has always been in the original Clements house and depicts scenes from Aesop’s Fables: On the long sides, the Fox and the Stork, while the vignettes on the short sides show the Fox and the Crow, and the Fox and the Grapes.  
The last and final room was the State Drawing Room.  This room contains two magnificent 18th-century Adam chimney pieces.  A chandelier hanging in the center of the room is made from brass in the Regency style and commemorates the Act of Union of 1801 by intertwining a shamrock, rose and thistle representing Ireland, England and Scotland.  
In the corner of the room is a gorgeous piano.  The ILE students were given the opportunity of a lifetime to tickle the ivories of the President’s Steinway.  Hannah eagerly stepped up to the piano bench and treated us all to a gorgeous song, followed by Savannah, Pete, Erin, Taryn and Piper.  These students are so talented.  They continue to amaze us each day!  While some students treated us to tunes in the State Drawing Room, others sat around a Connemara marble coffee table was also commissioned for President Bill Clinton’s visit in 2000.
Before we left, the Irish Life Experience made sure to take plenty of pictures to savor their cherished experience at Áras an Uachtaráin.  Thank you President McAleese and Mr. O’Neill!

title: Protected: Dublin Days
author: tharrison
content_raw:
The Irish Life Experience spent Tuesday in Dublin.  Students had the option of doing various tours throughout the day, such as the Book of Kells, Dublin Castle, Jameson Distillery, the Guinness Brewery, the National Art Museum, and St. Patrick’s Cathedral.  
Many spent their time wisely, exploring the historical sites of Dublin first, before shopping for Irish souvenirs.  Piper said she has enjoyed Dublin and Ireland so much, that she wants Taryn to convince her father to let her stay in Ireland permanently.  Ha!  Quite a few other students share Piper’s love and request for Ireland as well.  
After a full day of Dublin, students went back to King’s Hospital for dinner and to primp for Riverdance.  You should have seen these ILE’ers-absolutely stunning.  They are gorgeous kids!  
The Riverdance performance at the Gaiety was an innovative and exciting fusion of Irish and international dance.  It propelled traditional dance and music into the present day, and captured the imagination of the audience.  The ILE’ers could not stop raving about the fantastic show.  Hannah said it was phenomenal.  Scarlett was lucky enough to go back stage after the show and get signatures from all of the dancers.  How lucky!
All is well here in Dublin.  We have been very busy lately, so I apologize if the past few posts haven’t been quite as detailed.  Tomorrow we are heading north to Belfast, Carrick-a-rede Bridge, and the Giant’s Causeway.  I’m hoping to catch you up on Friday from today and tomorrow, so expect a long entry then, with plenty of beautiful pictures.  
To end tonight’s post, I had a conversation with a student today.  I just had to share.  This student asked me if there was such a thing as a happy ending in Irish history.  It was a great question, and I’ll give you the same answer I gave them.  The happy ending is the students that are with us on the Irish Life Experience.  Grandchildren and great grandchildren of immigrants who left with nothing.  Now returning home as interested and incredible young adults-thriving to learn more about Irish culture and incorporate it into their daily lives.  It’s simply amazing!

title: Protected: Kilmainham and Dublin
author: tharrison
content_raw:
“Beware of the Risen People that have Harried and Held, Ye that have Bullied and Bribed.”  This is the quote the Irish Life Experience students saw today inscribed over a door in Kilmainham Gaol by a prisoner during the Irish Civil War.  It quotes a speech by the iconic Irish nationalist Padraig Pearse who was executed on May 3, 1916 for his part in the Easter Rising. 
Kilmainham Gaol is a former prison, which is now a museum.  Kilmainham Gaol has played an important part in Irish history, as many leaders of Irish rebellions were imprisoned and some executed in the jail.  The jail has also been used as a set for several films, including In The Name Of The Father.  Over the 140 years it served as a prison, its cells held many of the most famous people involved in the campaign for Irish independence.  The leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising were held and executed here.  “It was very eerie being in the prison,” said Caitlin.  Piper thought it was an excellent historical tour, but very depressing.  “I enjoyed seeing the prison after watching Michael Collins,” said Clara.  
After the incredible tour of Kilmainham’s grim past, the ILE’ers had free time to wander the streets of Dublin.  They brought a packed lunch and some enjoyed the sunshine in Trinity square, before getting down to business to explore and shop.  Many arrived back to the bus with county jerseys, Ireland sweatshirts, Guinness souvenirs, and presents for family and friends.  Caitlin bought a Kilkenny jersey from where her family is from, while Maureen bought a Kerry jersey.  Caitlyn splurged and bought an Ireland football jersey, and said she can’t wait to wear it on St. Patrick’s Day.  Caroll’s, Elvery’s, Penney’s and Trinity Sweater purchases filled the bus back to King’s Hospital.  What a great day we had in Dublin.  
The night entailed a football game with the Italian and Spanish students at King’s Hospital and the famous Irish Life Experience Talent Show.  We have incredibly talented ILE’ers this year-more to come on that later!  They simply continue to amaze me.  
It’s past my bedtime, but will be back soon.  Good night from Eire!

title: Protected: Trad Music, Croker, and the Wee County
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello Irish Life Experience Families and Friends.  Just a quick recap with some lovely pictures of our ILE’ers!  Aren’t they gorgeous kids?  
Last night, Angie’s brother, Tom, came to visit us with his traditional Irish band from Belfast.  We were treated with magnificent tunes of jigs, hornpipes, and reels.  Music from banjos, buzukis, bodhrans, guitars, whistles and uilleann pipes echoed throughout the halls of King’s Hospital.  There was plenty of toe-tapping and it was music to our ears.  Tom and his friends introduced the students to each of the various unfamiliar instruments, before accompanying them to a few 3’s and 7’s they had learned in dance class.  Our two spectacular Irish dancers, Hannah and Scarlett, performed a few routines at the end of the sessiun.  As much as the students didn’t want the music to end, Tom and his band bid adieu.  Later, students watched In the Name of the Father with Daniel Day-Lewis, since it’s significant with the ILE visiting Kilmainham Gaol tomorrow.  It was a fantastic evening!  
Today, students had a lie-in and a relaxing morning.  This afternoon we went to Croke Park for the Leinster Gaelic Football Finals of Louth vs. Meath.  Louth has not won a Leinster Final since 1957 and Meath was the expected winner, so all of the students decided to cheer for the underdogs.  Many painted their faces Louth’s county colors of red and white and donned matching headbands.  The atmosphere was surreal with 50,000+ supporters.  There was so much energy and excitement amongst the crowds.  While Louth is known as the “Wee County,” they were mighty and put up a strong battle against Meath.  It was close throughout the game.  In the second half, Louth was up by one with a minute to spare and we thought it was a done deal.  A referee then allowed a last second illegal Meath goal which allowed them to defeat Louth 1-13 to 1-11.  Even though the ILE students were disappointed with the outcome of the game, they said it was one of the best experiences they have had thus far.  “I enjoyed watching the game after learning how to play it in Waterford,” said Scarlett.  “I’m so sad Louth lost.  However, I still had an incredible time,” said Paddy.  
Now back at King’s Hospital, the ILE’ers just went into the theatre to watch the World Cup Finals of Netherlands vs. Spain.  The groups seems to be split on whom to cheer for tonight.  Regardless, it should be an exciting match.  There is so much buzz right now.  
We are off on a tour tomorrow to Kilmainham Gaol and the students will then have free time in Dublin.  A lot of them are looking forward shopping galore on Grafton Street and in Temple Bar.
More to come, but Oiche Mhaith-Good Night…, for now!

title: Protected: Total Eclipse of the Heart
author: tharrison
content_raw:
Hello Irish Life Experience Families and Friends!  Greetings from Dublin.  
We arrived to the capital city on Thursday afternoon and were able to have a relaxing packed lunch in St. Stephen’s Green.  The students swapped ham with peanut butter and jelly sandwiches, sipped on chocolate milk, and devoured Hula Hoops-while sharing jokes with each other.  
Before it started spitting rain, Dan gave the students a special walking tour of his hometown.  On Dawson Street, he pointed out St. Ann’s Church and the National Museum of Ireland, where they have a spectacular James Joyce exhibit.  We turned left on Duke Street, and told the students about the famous Davy Byrne’s Literary Pub.  We then took a right onto the cobblestone of Grafton.  We followed our leader to the Molly Malone statue, also known as the “Tart with the Cart.”  A few students stopped to get a picture with Molly.  Both Caitlin and Piper said that they were familiar with Molly’s song and broke out in a brief snippet of “Cockles and Mussels.”  The herd headed up Westmoreland Street and we showed them the trendy Temple Bar, before we reached O’Connell Bridge.  As we crossed the Bridge, Dan told the students that it was the only bridge in the world that was as long as it is wide.  We pointed out a few shops of interest along the way, where students could pick up Irish jerseys and souvenirs.  Many are interested in getting county jerseys from where their relatives came from, so I’m sure Elvery’s will be seeing some business from our group this week;).  Eventually we reached the O’Connell Monument, the GPO (General Post Office), and the Spire or the Stiletto in the Ghetto.  Dan spoke about the significance of the GPO and the 1916 Rebellion, so the students found it very worthwhile.  “I enjoyed seeing the history of Dublin through walking its streets.  It felt as if I was finally in the heart and soul of Ireland,” said Caitlin.  Sydney said she can’t wait to return to explore the city even more.  We took a left on O’Connell and crossed over the Liffey again via the Ha’penny Bridge-into the popular Temple Bar.  We rounded the tour back to Grafton and finished up on Nassau Street in front of Trinity and the Book of Kells.  Luckily we were able to enjoy the streets of Dublin rain free.  We got on the bus in the nick of time-minutes before it started to down pour.  Phew!  We are definitely lucking out with the weather.
We drove to our new home of King’s Hospital in Palmerstown.  A suburb of Dublin, fifteen minutes outside the city center.  Students were able to get settled and were a little overwhelmed at first, since there are a few other groups of Italian and Spanish staying here.  We were very spoiled at Newtown, since we had the whole boarding school to roam freely by ourselves.  
On Thursday night, King’s Hospital arranged a disco for all of the campers.  The ILE’ers broke out some stellar moves, while Dan and Taryn impressed the students with their robot dance.  The students were exhausted after a long day of traveling, walking in Dublin, and dancing, so many were in bed early.
Friday was a typical class day for the students.  In literature, Pete spoke about Seamus Heaney.  In Gaelic, Dan taught them numbers.  A haon=1, A dó=2, A trí=3, A ceathair=4, A cúig=5, A sé=6, A seacht=7, A hocht=8, A naoi=9, A deich=10.  Dan spoke about Charles Stewart Parnell and the early 1800’s in Irish history.  In Irish studies, Taryn showed Reeling in the ’90’s DVD, where the students were able to see what Ireland was like when she first came to Ireland and why she fell in love with the country.  Dan then finished up the class day with Irish American history and talked about JFK.  
Friday night was a special treat for the students.  After dance and drama, we ALL went to see the premiere of Eclipse, from the Twilight Series.  Even though not all of the students were Twihearts, they all thought it was highly entertaining-whether they hated it or loved it.  Siobhan said it was incredible and she can’t wait for Breaking Dawn.  “I’m Team Victoria,” Siobhan said.  The students seemed divided on the Team Edward/Jacob controversy.  However, Bryan from Tenon Tours, said that he was on Team Charlie.  What a fun-filled night of vampires and werewolves in Ireland!
Today was the Irish Life Experience’s last class day.  Ahhh:(.  Angie talked about Frank O’Connor and read the short story of the Drunkard in her literature class.  Erin and Katie both said they loved the Drunkard and can’t wait to read more of Frank O’Connor’s stories.  After learning the numbers in Gaelic class on Friday, Dan played Irish Bingo with the ILE’ers.  Caitlin and Katie won!  Great job girls!  Moving on to Irish history, Dan talked about Ireland in the mid to late 1800’s and then had the students give a two minute presentation on a famous Irish American person in their lives for his Irish American history class.  Hannah, Paddy, and Piper spoke eloquently about their grandparents-a beautiful tribute to them.  Taryn finished her class speaking about the changes that Ireland has gone through in the past 20+ years and how the ILE students can preserve and promote Irish culture in America when they return.  Many are looking forward to sharing their new found knowledge and passion of Ireland with their families and friends.  Their love for the country and its people grows with each passing day.  They all said they can’t wait to return with the Irish Life Experience as Counselors!   
A conversation with a few girls last night, left me grinning from ear to ear.  There were a few tears and misty eyes, as they said it’s going by too quickly and that the Irish Life Experience is the best summer they have ever had!  This is why I love my job and know that we are doing something right, giving these young adults the education and experience of a lifetime.
