title: Protected: The ILE has the “Gift of the Gab!”
author: studentblog
content_raw:
The ILE kissed the Blarney Stone yesterday and now they have the “Gift of the Gab,” not that many of the students need any more of the “Gab” though.  Thursday marked our third tour of the month and we had perfect weather for the day.
We began the morning at Cahir Castle.  Once the stronghold of the powerful Butler family, the castle retains its impressive keep, tower and much of its original defensive structure.  It is one of Ireland’s largest and best preserved castles and is situated on a rocky island on the River Suir.  The students watched a short film on the history of the castle and then were given a guided tour.  They had a few minutes to take pictures and explore the grounds on their own.  “Cahir Castle was my favorite, because the tour was very interesting,” said Cailin.
We were back on the bus shortly after and making our way to Blarney-home of the Blarney Castle and the Blarney Woolen Mills.  The students walked up to the castle, climbed the narrow steps, and kissed the Blarney Stone.  We ate our packed lunches here and some of the students picked up a few souvenirs in the very popular Blarney Woolen Mills for friends and relatives.  Some even indulged in a .99 cone-delicious soft serve ice-cream that is definitely very addicting.  Kieran said, “I enjoyed Blarney, because there was a lot to see and do.”
Cork was our next destination and the students were given a few hours to eat dinner and shop.  Caroline walked along the River Lee and said it was a lot of fun.
On our long journey home, the ILE listened to Counselor Pete’s wonderful CD on the bus, as well as the Black Eyed Peas CD, so we were singing and dancing the whole way back to Waterford.  The students will be learning Irish tunes next week, so I’m sure we will hear the tunes of Molly Malone and the Wild Rover on future trips instead.
We made a quick stop in Youghal, where we stretched our legs and took advantage of a quick photo opportunity in front of the beautiful sea.  The students learned a quick trivia question, as Youhal is where the movie Moby Dick was filmed.
Today the students had classes.  In Irish Studies they learned about genealogy.  Taryn was able to look up family crests for each student and taught them how to research their own roots.
Teacher Dan had a game of Gaelic Bingo with the students with Grace, Sophia, and Tyler being the winners.
They learned about the Kennedy’s in Irish American history and started to learn about James Joyce in literature.  The students were introduced to Joyce by reading a story from the Dubliners.
Today, the students had free time in Waterford and many participated in the Scone Workshop this afternoon.  They were quite the bakers, but by the end of the Workshop, many were covered in as much flour as what was in the scones.  They will be able to taste their scones tonight at dinner time, which will be a treat!
A few groups of students have also been practicing some secret talents, as we will have a Talent Show tonight-which we are all looking forward to.
Enjoy the pictures!  All of the boys dressed up on Wednesday, so I was able to snap a few pictures of them in an impromptu modeling shoot-just in case you are wondering.
We are still having a wonderful time!

title: Protected: The ILE Becomes Hurling and Gaelic Football Pros!
author: studentblog
content_raw:
Today marked the third day of classes.  We can’t believe how fast time is flying!
This morning, ALL of the boys showed up in their dress pants/shirts/ties.  They all clean up well and looked very handsome.  They made it a point to sit in the front row of classes and were very professional.  When Teacher Dan walked into the classroom, they all stood up to acknowledge him as well.  I only wish I had a picture of them!
In Irish Studies, they learned about Ireland’s geography and geology.  We talked about the lakes, mountains, and rivers in Ireland and learned about peat.  A few kids thought it was Counselor Pete, Taryn was referring to, but now understand what peat in Ireland is:).  
In Gaelic, they learned how to count in preparation for Friday’s Bingo game.  A haon, a dó, a trí, a ceathair, a cúig…  Teacher Dan said they are doing well and participate a lot.  He said Cara, Caroline, Hannah, Kelsey, and Jamie were very good.  
For Irish history they learned about the Famine.  Teacher Dan also talked about the Famine, emigration, and the Civil War in Irish American history.  
Counselor Pete elaborated more on Patrick Cavanagh and students were assigned to write poems about him in his poetic scheme.  Counselor Pete said that Cailin and Jocelyn had great poems and he was very happy with their writing abilities!
We also had two special visitors today-Coaches from the Waterford GAA led by Eoin Breathnach.  The students loved it and had a blast!  You should have seem them take to the field.  They first learned Gaelic football, had a few competitions with basic passing movies, and then scrimmaged against each other. Conor, once again, picked it up very quickly and won the competition.  He’s a great athlete.  Jordan was runner-up.  Caroline also did well and has great coordination, but took a few spills in the process of diving for the ball.  Hannah also did well.  
The students then learned how to play hurling.  They put on their helmets, grabbed their hurleys and slithers, practiced dribbling the ball down the field, and then played a short game.  Eileen and Elysse liked hurling better, because it was more competitive.  Some of the students mentioned that they wanted to bring hurling sticks back home and practice in the states as well.  Cliff and Cailin picked hurling up very quickly.  
It was wonderful for the students to be able to learn how to play the Gaelic football and hurling, as we are going to the Leinster Finals on Sunday at Croke Park.  They now know the basics of the game and will be able to understand the match much better.
Tonight students will have their first dance/disco at the school.  Another group that is staying at the campus will be joining us, so everyone is looking forward to showing off their dance skills.  Ty and Cliff said they had some “awesome moves” to show us!  We can’t wait!
Everyone seems to be doing well.  A few complaints about the ketchup though, as they miss Heinz.  
Tomorrow we are off on another wonderful tour.  Cahir Castle, the Blarney Castle, Cork, and Youghal.  It’s going to be a great day!

title: Protected: Meet More ILE Staff
author: studentblog
content_raw:
Trying to describe Dan Parkinson is perhaps as difficult, and rewarding, as trying to encapsulate the beauty of a rose, the misty equanimity of a morning lake, or a child’s first steps.  His many facets and talents inspire all who get a chance to meet him.   After leaving home at the age of five on a competitive juggling scholarship, Dan had a chance to travel the finer parts of Ireland and Montenegro.  With a quick tour in the Maghreb with the Legionairres under his belt, Dan returned to Ireland to open up a little shop specializing in hard-to-find Japanese cinema.  A chance meeting with Taryn Harrison in the back of a Garda patrol car was all that Dan needed to know that he was ready to work with American students.
Don’t worry parents, sometimes we like to have a little fun, as Counselor Pete wrote Dan’s biography.  It’s all false:).
The real truth is that Dan originally hails from Dublin.  He’s a “Dub” through and through. He is a high school teacher at Terenure College in Dublin.  He has been working with American students for the past two years and loves it!  He has been to the states a few times, as he has relatives there and is looking forward to coming and visiting all of the new ILE students and their families in the future.  He’s also a Red Sox fan!
Dan teaches Gaelic, Irish American history, and Irish history to the students.  He’s an avid rugby fan and fantastic player and will be giving a Rugby Workshop to the students in Dublin.
He’s excited about this summer and is especially looking forward to impromptu music sessions with the students, as he has a beautiful voice.

title: Protected: Up Tipperary and Kilkenny!
author: studentblog
content_raw:
Today the ILE lucked out with beautiful weather for their second tour of the program.  The sun was shining for the majority of the day and it only sprinkled a few minutes while we were in Kilkenny.
We left for the Rock of Cashel-Carraig Phádraig-also known as Cashel of the Kings and St. Patrick’s Rock this morning.  The Rock of Cashel is a very popular tourist attraction and is a historic site in the heart of County Tipperary.  It served as a traditional seat of the kings of Munster for several hundred years prior to the Norman invasion.  Much of the fortress is being reconstructed inside, so students were able to walk around, climb on the rocks, and take pictures of the view-which is where the true beauty is-and eat their packed lunches.
After spending an hour at the Rock of Cashel, we then made our way to the town of Kilkenny.  Kilkenny-Cill Chainnigh-meaning Cell or Church of Canice is an energetic city situated on the banks of the River Nore. Along High Street are many shops and restaurants, so the students had free time and were able to wander and explore the city on their own.
We also went on a tour of the impressive Kilkenny Castle.  Teacher Dan was able to tell the students about the history of the castle and that is was the seat of the well known Butler family.  The castle was sold to the local Castle Restoration Committee in the 20th century for £50.  Part of the National Art Gallery is on display in the castle and there are ornamental gardens on the city side of the castle with extensive land and gardens to the front.  Jocelyn said, “I liked Kilkenny Castle, because there was so much to see.  The art gallery room was my favorite.”  Jordan also said he liked the art gallery the best.
We returned back to Newtown Boarding School tonight for dinner and a few students took Kendall’s Advanced Irish Dance Workshop.  Cliff and Ty even joined in.  They will be performing their routine for the talent show and possibly at a local Irish dance school in Waterford.
The winners of the Scavenger Hunt were also announced and the team that won was Cara, Caroline, Jamie, Jordan, and Mary.  Congratulations!  They won some Irish hats and blinking earrings.
A lot of the students are interested in watching Michael Collins tonight and tomorrow it’s a normal class day, where the students will be learning more about everything Irish.  Many are looking forward to the GAA-Gaelic Athletic Association-Workshop.  They will be learning how to play Gaelic football and hurling tomorrow from two amazing Waterford football coaches, so it will be fun.  They will scrimmage against each other.  My money is on whatever team Conor is on, because he was quite the athlete in ultimate frisbee.
Jocelyn also received a wonderful care package from her mother today.  Thank you Beverly.  She has been sharing her treats with all of the students and staff.  Taryn knows which room she is looking forward to going into for bed check tonight.  I love Swedish Fish:)!
That’s all for today.

title: Protected: 85 Degrees and Beautiful Weather!
author: studentblog
content_raw:
Just kidding…:)  Wouldn’t you know…, Ireland had gorgeous weather last month, but since we arrived, we have had quite a few rain showers.  Luckily, all of the students have good rain jackets that keep them dry and have been wonderful sports about it.  It hasn’t stopped us from having a great time.  “It’s always raining,” Sophia said.   
Today in Irish Studies they learned about the different counties and provinces in Ireland, along with some fun facts about Ireland.  Taryn agreed to give a prize to the student who could pronounce the longest city name in Ireland, which is Muckanaghederdauhaulia in Co. Galway.  Jordan was the winner. 
In Gaelic, they learned a few basics.  Hello-Dia dhuit.  How are you?-Conás átá tú?  What is your name?-Cad is ainm duit? Where are you from?-Cad as tú?  Hopefully by the time we get to the Gaeltacht on Inishmor, they will be able to have a simple conversation with some of the locals.  Eileen said, “I really love Gaelic and hope to be able to study it more when I return home.”
Their Irish history teacher, Dan, also taught them about the Normans and Vikings and the first time the British came to Ireland.    In Irish American history, they learned about the Ulster Scots and in literature, they were introduced to works from Patrick Cavanagh.
In drama, they continued working on their limericks of their assigned literary figures and in dance, once again, Irish Dance Teacher, Kendall was extremely impressed, as the students learned the Walls of Limerick! “It’s entertaining to watch everyone learn the steps in dance class,” Elysse said.
Tonight, Counselor Kendall organized a scavenger hunt for the students in Waterford.  Some teams did very well and found almost everything.  Some of the things on the list were to find the cheapest fish and chips in town, to have someone serenade them on the streets of Waterford, and to find a recipe from a local resident.  The winners will be announced tomorrow and will receive a prize for their efforts.  
We are off to the Rock of Cashel tomorrow and to Kilkenny Castle.  They will have some time to explore the wonderful city of Kilkenny which I’m sure the students will enjoy as well.

title: Protected: Happy 4th of July!
author: studentblog
content_raw:
Hello from Waterford and Happy 4th of July from the ILE!
The students woke up bright and early for breakfast and to start their first day of classes.  A few of them have discovered the delicious Irish brown bread and tea, which will most likely become a staple in their daily diets. They all seem a bit more awake today and recovered from their jet leg, after getting a good night’s sleep.
They had an introduction to Gaelic, Irish American History, Irish History, and Literature with their Irish teachers this morning and a detailed orientation about what to expect on campus in Waterford and throughout the trip.
After lunch, the students were free to wander around and explore Waterford City on their own for a few hours.  A few went to check their e-mail at an internet cafe, shop, take pictures and enjoy a local music festival.
The students returned home for a special 4th of July BBQ.  They were serenaded by Counselor Pete on his guitar, while chatting and eating American flag cookies from Jamie’s mom.  Thank you Melissa!
 
Dinner was followed by Drama and Dance.  In Drama, they were broken into groups of important Irish literary figures and assigned to write limericks about them.  In Dance, they learned the Seige of Ennis. Kendall, their Irish dance teacher was very impressed, as they learned their 3’s and 7’s very quickly, while Irish dancers, Cailin, Eileen, Grace, and Kelsey demonstrated their amazing dancing talents to the rest of the group.
The evening activities included ultimate frisbee with Conor being the MVP and winning the game for his team, a movie, and some comfort American food-Domino’s pizza, Coke, and chocolate.
Even though there were no fireworks, the celebration was good and everyone was happy.
Off to bed now to get some sleep before our first tour of the program tomorrow-the Waterford Crystal Store and the seaside town of Tramore.  If the weather permits, the brave at heart might go swimming in the frigid water.
More tomorrow…

title: Protected: The ILE has landed in Eire!
author: studentblog
content_raw:
The ILE left JFK last night at 9:40 PM and arrived Dublin Airport safe and sound at 9:10 AM this morning.  All of the students made the Aer Lingus flight and there weren’t too many delays or lost luggage.  Phew!  We even lucked out and had a brand new plane with tv’s in every seat, so the students were lucky enough to watch and assortment of movies and play games to help pass time during the six hour flight.
The students met their Irish teachers and traveled to Glendalough-Valley of the Two Lakes-in the heart of the Wicklow Mountains.  For those of you who have seen the movie, PS I Love You, this is where some of it was filmed.  It’s a beautiful area of Ireland and rich in history.  It’s a Monastic site with a Round Tower.  The students walked around the smaller lake, stretched their legs, got some fresh air, and ate a packed lunch, before getting on the bus to travel to Waterford-their post until the 12th.
The students are jet legged and the exhaustion is finally setting in.  They arrived Newtown Boarding School and are getting settled, taking showers, and depositing their passports and money into the ILE Bank.  We will be eating dinner soon, having a brief Orientation, and doing some fun ice-breakers to get to know each other.  We have a feeling it’s going to be a very early night, as the eyelids of many are getting very heavy.
They are ALL wonderful students and doing well.
We will try to post a few pictures later.
Slan.

title: From student to counselor
author: tharrison
content_raw:
It is somewhat difficult to describe one of the most transformative experiences of my life, but what Taryn Harrison asks, I do willingly.  Going to Ireland under the guidance of Taryn and Angie is truly an eye-opening experience.  Having participated as a student in 2002 and then coming back as counselor in 2008 were equally rewarding on a myriad of experiential levels.  As a student, I had the chance to be away from not only my country, but also my parents.  Those few summer weeks as a junior in high school set me in a direction which I still follow today.  That trip opened me up to Irish culture and history, but most importantly for my own life, Irish literature and music.  I also made many life-long friendships which were formed during those dream-like weeks when I was sixteen in Ireland.  I should probably not admit this, but I cried openly and freely at the airport when the group came back to the states (and I am of the opinion that men should cry only when something falls on them).
When I came back to the program as a counselor six years later, I had a whole new view of what goes into Irish Life Experience.  As a student, I simply thought the teachers were good enough to wet my appetite for what they discussed.  To work and live with these teachers as an adult, however, demonstrated that these people were not simply trying to keep the kids entertained, but rather were prepared and professional to the highest degree.  Aside from the didactic facets, I was amazed at the emotional and personal investment in the students and their welfare.  I cannot recommend this program highly enough.  This is a trip that I found myself, like almost everyone else, incredibly apprehensive about before going on, and then uncommonly sad to be leaving.  It offers a chance for responsibility and growth that dwarfs most other opportunities for young adults.
-Peter Ford, Chatham, NJ – Student 2002, Counselor 2006

title: When strangers became friends
author: tharrison
content_raw:
My trip to Ireland was an amazing experience that provided me with many memories I will cherish for the rest of my life. It opened my eyes not only to the richness of Irish culture, but also to the vastness of my own country. I became close friends with people from places like Canada, Washington, and California, as well as New Jersey, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania. I still keep in touch with these friends and we have had several reunions since our time in Ireland.  Though we were only together there for a month, we shared experiences that bound us together forever.
I learned and saw so much throughout the trip that it is hard to pinpoint a favorite excursion, lesson, or activity. We would spend one day playing “Simon Says” in Irish and the next trekking across the
Giant’s Causeway or signing the peace wall in Belfast. We became expert scone bakers and set dancers, connoisseurs of Irish poetry, and masters of Dublin’s public transportation system. When we weren’t in the classroom studying the conflict in Northern Ireland or the War of Independence, we were in our drama groups planning skits on the lives of famous Irish personas like Michael Collins, St. Patrick, and Finn McCool.
What truly made my experience in Ireland a special one, however, were the trip leaders. When I arrived at the airport I was greeted by Taryn, who already knew the names of every group member and made us all feel so comfortable and welcome. Both Taryn and Angie did an amazing job of exposing us to different aspects of Irish culture and fostering within us a love of Ireland as great as their own.
– Laura Travers, Eastchester, NY – Student, 2006

title: An enlightening experience
author: tharrison
content_raw:
I feel lucky and blessed to have experienced a comprehensive and amazing trip to Ireland at such a young age. Traveling around the magical country of Ireland was the most enlightening experience of my life and Taryn and Angie made it even more enriching. My experience in Ireland with these two stunning women taught me to embrace my heritage and be proud of where I come from. I felt right at home in Ireland and by the time I came home a month later I knew so much more about The Emerald Isle because Angie and Taryn made it a fun learning experience.
The group of high-schoolers that are lucky enough to go on this trip are very special people, I made four best friends in my month there. We fostered such a strong bond that we all still keep in touch with each other. Taryn is such an amazing person and I have learned so much from her since I’ve met her. I could not have had a better experience in Ireland with Angie and Taryn. I would go on the trip again in an instant.
– Meghan, New Jersey – Student, 2007

title: The Summer that Changed My Life
author: tharrison
content_raw:
My 16th summer was the summer that changed my life. That was because, It was the summer that I fell in love,not with a person, but with my culture and my heritage. It was the summer that I spent a month in Ireland with some of the greatest teachers, and the greatest people I have ever met.
Through this summer study abroad program, I not only learned about the history of my culture, or about the literature, but also about the people and how they live. I was lucky enough to experience the mythical sites that I had only ever read about in books, or heard about in stories from my grandmother.
One of the things that made my time in Ireland so valuable, were the counselors and the teachers that made me eager to learn, as well as explore the quaint cities we were situated in. Taryn and Vinnie encouraged us to try new things and to learn as much as we could, while Angie thrust us into Irish culture with her sharp wit and lilting brogue that brought the stories of Ireland’s writers to life for us.
This unique study abroad program not only helped to grow in knowledge but as a person as well. I learned to be an adult, because I was treated like one. I lived with many other young adults, and at certain times during the trip, I was responsible for shopping for and cooking my own food, on a budget that had been given to us. When the time came to leave Ireland, I was crying because the time had gone way too quickly.
My time in Ireland not only instilled in me a love of my culture and the country of my ancestors but a thirst to continue seeking knowledge about Ireland and her people. This program also provided me with some of the best friends I have ever known. Although our homes span hundreds even thousands of miles, we have never let the distance stop us from staying involved in each others lives. I not only keep in touch with the students but with my teachers and counselors as well. They have remained mentors to me, long after the trip was over. I will never forget that summer, and I will always cherish it, as one of the most important experiences in my young adult life.
– Maureen McNulty, New York – Student, 2007
